sections.title: Amazon Athena
sections.summary: Serverless SQL on data in Amazon S3, priced by the data each query scans.

items.name: Exploring and building training sets
items.summary: Query raw data in S3 with SQL to profile it and create training datasets.
items.details: Athena reads tables defined in the Glue Data Catalog and can write results back to S3 with CREATE TABLE AS SELECT (CTAS), which is a quick way to build a filtered training set in Parquet.
items.example: An ML engineer runs a CTAS query that selects 12 months of labeled transactions into Parquet for training.
items.tip: SQL on S3 with no servers → Athena. It also queries the Feature Store offline store.

items.name: Scanning less data
items.summary: Parquet or ORC, compression, and partitions cut cost and time because Athena bills per byte scanned.
items.details: Columnar formats let Athena read only the columns a query needs, and partitions (for example by date) let it skip whole folders.
items.example: Partitioning clickstream data by day lets a query for last week scan 7 folders instead of 3 years.
items.tip: Rising Athena costs → convert to Parquet and partition on common filters.

sections.title: Amazon Data Firehose
sections.summary: Fully managed delivery of streaming data to S3, Redshift, OpenSearch, and other destinations.

items.name: Buffer and deliver streams
items.summary: Firehose batches records by size or time and writes them to a destination with no servers.
items.details: Producers send records (or Firehose reads from a Kinesis data stream), Firehose buffers them, optionally compresses or transforms them, and delivers files to S3 and other targets. It scales automatically.
items.example: Clickstream events land in S3 every 5 minutes for nightly feature engineering.
items.tip: Near-real-time delivery to S3 with no code → Firehose. Millisecond custom processing → Kinesis Data Streams consumers.

items.name: Format conversion and transformation
items.summary: Convert JSON to Parquet or ORC with a Glue schema, or transform records with a Lambda function.
items.details: Record format conversion uses a table schema from the Glue Data Catalog. A Lambda transformation can clean or enrich each record before delivery.
items.example: JSON sensor events are converted to Parquet so Athena queries scan less data.
items.tip: Streaming JSON → Parquet in S3 → Firehose record format conversion.

sections.title: Amazon EMR
sections.summary: Managed Apache Spark, Hadoop, Hive, and Presto on clusters, on EKS, or serverless.

items.name: Large-scale Spark processing
items.summary: Run existing Spark or PySpark feature engineering at petabyte scale with control of the cluster.
items.details: EMR suits teams that already have Spark code, need custom libraries or configurations, or process very large datasets. EMR Serverless removes cluster management.
items.example: A team runs hundreds of existing PySpark jobs with custom JARs on EMR.
items.tip: Existing Spark/Hadoop code or full cluster control → EMR. Serverless ETL with less setup → Glue.

sections.title: AWS Glue
sections.summary: Serverless data integration: Spark ETL jobs, crawlers, the Data Catalog, and sensitive data detection.

items.name: Serverless ETL jobs
items.summary: Join, clean, and reshape data from S3, JDBC databases, and streams with serverless Spark.
items.details: Glue jobs read sources through connections (for example RDS over JDBC), transform them, and write results such as Parquet to S3. Triggers and workflows schedule and chain jobs. Worker types such as G.2X add memory.
items.example: A nightly Glue job joins RDS customer records with S3 purchase history for training.
items.tip: Scheduled joins across sources with no servers → Glue ETL.

items.name: Crawlers and the Data Catalog
items.summary: Crawlers infer schemas and register tables that Athena, EMR, Redshift, and Firehose use.
items.details: The Data Catalog is the central metadata store. Crawlers scan data stores and create or update table definitions and partitions.
items.example: A crawler adds new daily partitions so Athena queries see the latest data.

items.name: Job bookmarks
items.summary: Bookmarks track processed data so each run reads only new files.
items.details: Without bookmarks, a job reprocesses everything on every run. With bookmarks, incremental runs are faster and cheaper.
items.example: A job that reprocessed 900 GB nightly now reads only the day’s new files.
items.tip: Glue job slowly reprocessing all history → enable job bookmarks.

items.name: Detect PII transform
items.summary: Find sensitive data in columns and mask, hash, or redact it during ETL.
items.details: Glue’s sensitive data detection identifies entities such as names, emails, and card numbers in columns, and the job can mask or hash them before writing training data.
items.example: Email addresses are hashed before the data is used for model training.
items.tip: Mask PII in tabular pipelines → Glue Detect PII. Find PII across buckets → Macie.

sections.title: AWS Glue DataBrew
sections.summary: Visual, no-code data preparation with 250+ transforms saved as reusable recipes.

items.name: Recipes and recipe jobs
items.summary: Clean and normalize data visually, then run the saved steps as a scheduled job.
items.details: Analysts build recipes (for example remove duplicates, fix date formats, impute values) in a visual editor and run them on full datasets as recipe jobs.
items.example: Business analysts standardize product data weekly without writing code.
items.tip: No-code cleaning with reusable steps → DataBrew.

items.name: Profile jobs and data quality rules
items.summary: Column statistics, distributions, correlations, and rule checks without code.
items.details: A profile job reports missing values, distinct counts, and distributions. Data quality rulesets check conditions such as completeness or value ranges.
items.example: An analyst profiles a new dataset before deciding which features to build.

sections.title: AWS Glue Data Quality
sections.summary: Rule-based data quality checks (DQDL) in the Data Catalog and inside Glue ETL jobs.

items.name: Data quality rules in pipelines
items.summary: Evaluate rules such as Completeness, Uniqueness, and ColumnValues, then fail the job or route bad rows.
items.details: Glue Data Quality uses the Data Quality Definition Language (DQDL). It can recommend rules from data statistics, score datasets, and stop an ETL job when rules fail so bad data never reaches training.
items.example: A job stops when a key column is more than 5% null, protecting the weekly retraining.
items.tip: Stop bad data from reaching training → Glue Data Quality rules in the ETL job.

sections.title: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
sections.summary: Real-time streams with custom consumers; capacity in shards (provisioned) or on-demand mode.

items.name: Streams and consumers
items.summary: Producers write records; consumers such as Lambda, Flink, or custom apps process them within milliseconds.
items.details: Records are ordered per shard by partition key and kept for 24 hours by default (up to 365 days). Enhanced fan-out gives each consumer dedicated read throughput.
items.example: A Lambda function reads card transactions from a stream to update fraud features.
items.tip: Real-time custom processing of streams → Kinesis Data Streams.

items.name: Shards and partition keys
items.summary: Each shard has write and read limits; a skewed partition key creates a hot shard.
items.details: Throttling (ProvisionedThroughputExceededException) on one shard usually means a low-cardinality partition key. Use high-cardinality keys, add shards, or switch to on-demand mode.
items.example: Using device ID instead of device model as the partition key spreads writes evenly.
items.tip: Hot shard → better partition key; overall capacity → more shards or on-demand.

sections.title: AWS Lake Formation
sections.summary: Centralized, fine-grained permissions for data lake tables in the Glue Data Catalog.

items.name: Column-, row-, and cell-level access
items.summary: Grant access to specific columns or rows, enforced by Athena, EMR, Redshift Spectrum, and Glue.
items.details: Lake Formation permissions and LF-tags let data owners share tables without copying data, while hiding sensitive columns from some users.
items.example: Fraud analysts query a customer table without seeing date of birth or address.
items.tip: Hide columns or rows in a data lake → Lake Formation, not S3 bucket policies.

sections.title: Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink
sections.summary: Stateful stream processing with Apache Flink (Java, Python, SQL), fully managed.

items.name: Windowed, stateful streaming features
items.summary: Compute rolling counts, sessions, and joins over streams continuously.
items.details: Flink keeps state and supports time windows, so it can compute features such as “transactions in the last 5 minutes per card” and write them to the Feature Store or other sinks.
items.example: A ride-sharing app computes trips per driver over a sliding 15-minute window.
items.tip: Stateful or windowed stream aggregation → Managed Service for Apache Flink.

sections.title: Amazon OpenSearch Service
sections.summary: Search and analytics engine with k-NN vector search; managed domains or OpenSearch Serverless.

items.name: Vector database for RAG
items.summary: k-NN indexes (HNSW or IVF) store embeddings for low-latency similarity search.
items.details: OpenSearch is a common Bedrock knowledge base vector store, either as an OpenSearch Serverless vector collection or a managed domain. It scales to billions of vectors with millisecond queries.
items.example: A support assistant retrieves the 5 most similar troubleshooting passages in under 50 ms.
items.tip: Low-latency, high-QPS vector search with rich filtering → OpenSearch.

items.name: Hybrid search
items.summary: Combine lexical (BM25) keyword matching with vector similarity for better ranking.
items.details: Hybrid queries help when users search for exact identifiers, such as part numbers or error codes, that embeddings represent poorly.
items.example: Queries for “XR-2044-B” match the exact part number while semantic queries still work.
items.tip: Exact terms missed by vector search → hybrid search.

sections.title: Amazon Quick
sections.summary: AWS’s business intelligence suite, including Quick Sight dashboards (formerly Amazon QuickSight).

items.name: Dashboards for model and business metrics
items.summary: Visualize predictions, drift trends, and business KPIs for stakeholders.
items.details: Quick Sight dashboards can read from Athena, Redshift, and S3. AWS’s recommended replacement for Model Monitor uses Quick Sight governance dashboards for drift and model quality trends.
items.example: Executives view weekly churn predictions and model accuracy trends in a dashboard.
items.tip: Business-facing dashboards → Amazon Quick (Quick Sight). Operational metrics and alarms → CloudWatch.

sections.title: Amazon Redshift
sections.summary: Petabyte-scale data warehouse with SQL analytics, Redshift ML, and Spectrum queries on S3.

items.name: Training data from the warehouse
items.summary: Use SQL to aggregate features or UNLOAD results to S3 in Parquet for training.
items.details: Redshift holds curated business data. UNLOAD exports query results to S3; Redshift ML can train models with SageMaker AI from SQL (CREATE MODEL).
items.example: An analyst creates a churn model with CREATE MODEL without leaving SQL.

items.name: Natural-language questions over tables
items.summary: Bedrock knowledge bases can use Redshift as a structured data store and generate SQL.
items.details: Structured data retrieval converts a question into SQL, runs it against the live tables, and returns the result to the model. Vector search isn’t suited to sums and groupings.
items.example: “What was Q3 revenue by region?” is answered from the live warehouse tables.
items.tip: Questions about numbers in tables → structured retrieval (NL to SQL), not vector RAG.

sections.title: Amazon EventBridge
sections.summary: Serverless event bus and scheduler that routes AWS and custom events to targets.

items.name: Event-driven MLOps
items.summary: SageMaker emits events (training job, pipeline execution, model package state) that rules route to targets.
items.details: Rules match events and start targets such as a SageMaker pipeline, CodePipeline, Lambda, or SNS. Common patterns: start deployment when a model is approved, alert when a pipeline fails, retrain on a schedule.
items.example: A model package changing to Approved starts the deployment pipeline.
items.tip: React to SageMaker state changes or run on a schedule → EventBridge.

items.name: EventBridge Scheduler
items.summary: One-time or recurring schedules (cron or rate) that invoke AWS targets.
items.details: Scheduler starts jobs, pipelines, or knowledge base syncs on a timetable without servers.
items.example: A weekly drift check runs every Sunday at 02:00.

sections.title: Amazon Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow (Amazon MWAA)
sections.summary: Managed Apache Airflow for teams that orchestrate pipelines as DAGs.

items.name: Existing Airflow DAGs
items.summary: Run Airflow without managing servers; Airflow has operators for SageMaker AI, Glue, and EMR.
items.details: MWAA suits organizations that already use Airflow for data engineering and want ML steps in the same DAGs.
items.example: Training and batch scoring tasks are added to the company’s existing nightly data DAG.
items.tip: Existing Airflow → MWAA. ML-native with lineage → SageMaker Pipelines. General AWS workflows → Step Functions.

sections.title: Amazon SNS
sections.summary: Pub/sub messaging and notifications: email, SMS, Lambda, SQS, and HTTP endpoints.

items.name: Alerts and async results
items.summary: Notify teams when alarms fire or pipelines fail, and notify apps when async inference finishes.
items.details: CloudWatch alarms, EventBridge rules, and SageMaker asynchronous inference can publish to SNS topics.
items.example: An async endpoint publishes a success message so the app can fetch the result from S3.

sections.title: Amazon SQS
sections.summary: Fully managed message queues that decouple producers and consumers.

items.name: Buffering inference requests
items.summary: Queue work so consumers process it at their own pace; dead-letter queues hold failed messages.
items.details: SQS absorbs bursts between components, for example uploads waiting for batch processing. A dead-letter queue keeps messages that repeatedly fail for later inspection.
items.example: Document uploads are queued and processed by workers that call a model.

sections.title: AWS Step Functions
sections.summary: Serverless workflow orchestration with retries, branching, and 200+ service integrations.

items.name: Orchestrating ML and data steps
items.summary: Chain Glue jobs, SageMaker jobs, Bedrock calls, and knowledge base syncs with error handling.
items.details: Step Functions waits for jobs to finish (.sync integrations), retries on failure, and branches on results. It’s useful when a workflow spans many AWS services.
items.example: ETL runs, then the knowledge base syncs, and SNS alerts the team if any step fails.
items.tip: Multi-service workflow with retries and error handling → Step Functions.

sections.title: AWS Billing and Cost Management
sections.summary: Bills, payments, cost allocation tags, and the cost management tools in one console.

items.name: Cost allocation tags
items.summary: Activate tags so costs can be grouped by team, project, or model in reports.
items.details: Tags on SageMaker endpoints, training jobs, and Bedrock application inference profiles let Cost Explorer split costs by owner.
items.example: Each team’s endpoints are tagged team=fraud or team=search for chargeback.
items.tip: Show costs per team or app → tag resources and activate cost allocation tags.

sections.title: AWS Budgets
sections.summary: Cost and usage budgets with alerts on actual or forecasted spend, plus automated budget actions.

items.name: Budget alerts
items.summary: Email or SNS alerts when actual or forecasted spend crosses a threshold.
items.details: Budgets can track total cost, a service such as SageMaker AI or Bedrock, or a tag.
items.example: An alert fires when forecasted Bedrock spend reaches 80% of the monthly budget.

items.name: Budget actions
items.summary: Automatically apply an IAM policy or SCP, or stop instances, when a budget is exceeded.
items.details: Actions enforce limits instead of only alerting, for example denying new SageMaker resources once spend hits 100%.
items.example: The ML sandbox account can’t start new training jobs after its budget is spent.
items.tip: Alert AND enforce → Budgets with budget actions.

sections.title: AWS Cost Explorer
sections.summary: Visualize and analyze historical costs and usage, with forecasts and filters.

items.name: Finding ML cost drivers
items.summary: Filter by service, usage type, tag, or Region to see what drives SageMaker AI and Bedrock costs.
items.details: Usage types reveal details such as idle notebook hours, endpoint instance hours, or input versus output tokens.
items.example: Cost Explorer shows GPU Studio spaces running all weekend.

items.name: Cost Anomaly Detection
items.summary: ML-based detection of unusual spend with alerts.
items.details: Cost Anomaly Detection learns normal spending patterns and alerts on spikes, for example an agent stuck in a loop.
items.example: A sudden jump in Bedrock spend triggers an anomaly alert the same day.

sections.title: AWS Batch
sections.summary: Managed batch computing that queues and runs containerized jobs on EC2, Spot, or Fargate.

items.name: Large batch workloads
items.summary: Run many containerized jobs, including GPU jobs, with queues and priorities.
items.details: Batch handles scheduling and scaling of compute environments for jobs such as simulations or bulk preprocessing.
items.example: Thousands of image preprocessing jobs run overnight on Spot capacity.

sections.title: Amazon EC2
sections.summary: Virtual servers; the instance families behind SageMaker AI choices.

items.name: Instance families for ML
items.summary: G and P (NVIDIA GPUs), Inf (Inferentia), Trn (Trainium), C (compute), M (general), R (memory), T (burstable).
items.details: SageMaker AI instance types use the same families with an ml. prefix. Inferentia (ml.inf2) lowers inference cost, Trainium (ml.trn1/trn2) lowers training cost, and CPU families suit tree models and small models.
items.example: An XGBoost model moves from ml.g5 to ml.c7g and costs far less with the same latency.
items.tip: Pick the cheapest family that the model actually needs.

items.name: AWS ML chips
items.summary: Inferentia for inference and Trainium for training, both programmed with the AWS Neuron SDK.
items.details: Models must be compiled with Neuron to run on these chips.
items.example: A transformer compiled with Neuron serves on Inf2 at a lower cost per request.

sections.title: AWS Lambda
sections.summary: Run code on events without servers; billed per request and duration (up to 15 minutes).

items.name: Glue code for ML systems
items.summary: Transform stream records, call endpoints or Bedrock, implement agent tools, and react to events.
items.details: Lambda is common for stateless per-record transforms on Kinesis, lightweight preprocessing, reward functions for reinforcement fine-tuning, and tools behind AgentCore Gateway.
items.example: A Lambda function converts temperatures and enriches each Kinesis record.
items.tip: Short, stateless, event-driven code → Lambda. Long-running agent sessions → AgentCore Runtime.

sections.title: Amazon ECR
sections.summary: Managed container registry for training and inference images.

items.name: Versioned images
items.summary: Store custom training and serving images; use unique tags or digests and tag immutability.
items.details: SageMaker AI pulls custom images from ECR. Immutable, unique tags make rollbacks reliable; lifecycle policies remove old images.
items.example: Each build is tagged with its Git commit ID, and the repository blocks tag overwrites.
items.tip: Overwritten “latest” tags break rollbacks → immutable unique tags.

items.name: Image scanning
items.summary: Enhanced scanning with Amazon Inspector finds vulnerabilities in OS and language packages.
items.details: Scan on push and continuously, and send findings to EventBridge so pipelines can block critical vulnerabilities.
items.example: A deployment stage fails when the new image has a critical CVE.

sections.title: Amazon ECS
sections.summary: AWS-native container orchestration on EC2 or Fargate.

items.name: Running AI applications
items.summary: Host the API layer of AI apps, model servers, or agents in containers.
items.details: ECS tasks use IAM task roles for temporary credentials, which is the recommended way for a service to call Bedrock.
items.example: A RAG API on ECS Fargate calls Bedrock with its task role.

sections.title: Amazon EKS
sections.summary: Managed Kubernetes for teams standardized on Kubernetes tooling.

items.name: ML on Kubernetes
items.summary: Run training or inference on Kubernetes; SageMaker HyperPod can also use EKS for orchestration.
items.details: EKS fits organizations that already run Kubernetes. It adds more operational work than managed SageMaker AI endpoints.
items.example: A platform team runs its inference servers on EKS GPU node groups.
items.tip: Least operational overhead usually favors SageMaker AI or Bedrock over EKS.

sections.title: Amazon DocumentDB
sections.summary: MongoDB-compatible document database with vector search support.

items.name: JSON documents and vectors
items.summary: Store JSON documents and run vector similarity search alongside them.
items.details: Useful when an application already stores its data as MongoDB-style documents.
items.example: Product documents and their embeddings live in one DocumentDB collection.

sections.title: Amazon DynamoDB
sections.summary: Serverless key-value and document database with single-digit millisecond latency.

items.name: Low-latency lookups and state
items.summary: Store features, session state, and metadata that applications read in milliseconds.
items.details: Items are limited to 400 KB, so large files belong in S3 with a pointer in DynamoDB.
items.example: Episode metadata in DynamoDB points to audio files in S3.

items.name: Export to S3
items.summary: Export a full table to S3 from point-in-time recovery backups without using read capacity.
items.details: The export feature needs PITR enabled and produces files that Glue or Athena can read for training.
items.example: A 2 TB production table is exported for training with no impact on live traffic.
items.tip: Copy a table for training without throttling production → DynamoDB export to S3.

sections.title: Amazon ElastiCache
sections.summary: Managed in-memory caching (Valkey, Redis OSS, Memcached).

items.name: Caching and fast state
items.summary: Cache frequent results or keep short-lived session state with microsecond latency.
items.details: In-memory storage is fast but the most expensive per GB, so it suits hot data rather than large archives.
items.example: Frequently asked questions and their answers are cached to avoid repeated model calls.

sections.title: Amazon Neptune
sections.summary: Managed graph database; Neptune Analytics supports GraphRAG with Bedrock knowledge bases.

items.name: GraphRAG
items.summary: Combine vector search with a knowledge graph to answer multi-hop questions across documents.
items.details: Graph retrieval follows relationships between entities (drugs, trials, compounds) that plain vector search misses.
items.example: A research assistant answers which trials studied drugs that interact with a compound.
items.tip: Multi-hop relationship questions → GraphRAG with Neptune Analytics.

sections.title: Amazon RDS
sections.summary: Managed relational databases; PostgreSQL engines support the pgvector extension.

items.name: Relational data for training
items.summary: Read training data over JDBC with Glue, or export snapshots to S3.
items.details: Avoid heavy analytical queries on the production primary; use a read replica or an export.
items.example: A Glue job reads customer tables from an RDS read replica nightly.

items.name: Vectors in PostgreSQL (pgvector)
items.summary: Store embeddings beside relational rows in RDS for PostgreSQL or Aurora PostgreSQL.
items.details: pgvector adds a vector column type and similarity search with HNSW or IVFFlat indexes, so semantic search can join with existing tables in SQL. Aurora PostgreSQL can be a Bedrock knowledge base vector store.
items.example: Product rows gain an embedding column for semantic search without a new database.
items.tip: Vectors next to existing PostgreSQL data → pgvector.

sections.title: AWS CDK
sections.summary: Define infrastructure in Python, TypeScript, and other languages; synthesizes CloudFormation.

items.name: Infrastructure as code with programming languages
items.summary: Use loops, classes, and reusable constructs for endpoints, roles, and pipelines.
items.details: The CDK generates CloudFormation templates, so deployments, rollbacks, and drift detection work the same way.
items.example: An ML platform team publishes a construct that creates a standard secure endpoint.

sections.title: AWS CodeArtifact
sections.summary: Managed package repository for pip, npm, Maven, and more, with upstream proxies.

items.name: Private Python packages
items.summary: Share internal libraries and cache approved PyPI packages for builds and training jobs.
items.details: Builds and VPC-isolated jobs can install packages from CodeArtifact instead of the public internet.
items.example: Training jobs in private subnets install packages through a CodeArtifact repository.

sections.title: AWS CodeBuild
sections.summary: Managed build service: runs tests, builds images, and executes scripts from a buildspec.

items.name: Build and test stages
items.summary: Run unit tests, build and push images, and start pipelines or evaluations.
items.details: The CodeBuild service role needs permissions for everything the build touches, such as ECR push (and privileged mode for Docker builds).
items.example: A build fails with AccessDenied on ECR until the service role gets push permissions.
items.tip: CodeBuild permission errors → fix the service role.

sections.title: AWS CodeCommit
sections.summary: Managed private Git repositories; back to full general availability since November 2025.

items.name: Source control on AWS
items.summary: Host Git repositories that trigger CodePipeline on changes.
items.details: CodeCommit was closed to new customers in 2024 and returned to general availability in November 2025. Many teams use GitHub or GitLab through CodeConnections instead.
items.example: A merge to main in CodeCommit starts a training pipeline.

sections.title: AWS CodeConnections
sections.summary: Connects CodePipeline and other services to GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket (formerly CodeStar Connections).

items.name: Third-party Git sources
items.summary: Use an external repository as a pipeline source without storing credentials in the pipeline.
items.details: A connection is authorized once and then used by CodePipeline or SageMaker projects.
items.example: Commits to GitHub start CodePipeline through a connection.
items.tip: GitHub/GitLab as a pipeline source → CodeConnections.

sections.title: AWS CodeDeploy
sections.summary: Automated deployments to EC2, Lambda, and ECS with traffic shifting and rollback.

items.name: Application deployments
items.summary: Canary or linear traffic shifting for Lambda and ECS, with automatic rollback on alarms.
items.details: For SageMaker AI endpoints, deployment guardrails provide the equivalent blue/green and rolling options natively.
items.example: A Lambda inference wrapper shifts 10% of traffic to a new version before full release.
items.tip: SageMaker endpoint updates → deployment guardrails; Lambda/ECS/EC2 apps → CodeDeploy.

sections.title: AWS CodePipeline
sections.summary: Continuous delivery pipelines that chain source, build, test, approval, and deploy stages.

items.name: ML CI/CD pipelines
items.summary: Automate code and infrastructure releases, including manual approval stages.
items.details: Typical MLOps: source (CodeConnections) → build and test (CodeBuild) → deploy infrastructure (CloudFormation) → approval → production.
items.example: An approved model triggers a pipeline that deploys to staging, tests, and then to production.

sections.title: AWS X-Ray
sections.summary: Distributed tracing that shows latency and errors for each hop of a request.

items.name: Tracing AI applications
items.summary: See time spent in API Gateway, Lambda, knowledge base retrieval, and model calls.
items.details: X-Ray and CloudWatch Application Signals help find which downstream call slows a request. AgentCore Observability provides agent-specific traces.
items.example: A trace shows 9 of 12 seconds spent in an unindexed database lookup.
items.tip: Per-hop latency in a distributed request → X-Ray.

sections.title: Amazon SageMaker AI
sections.summary: Fully managed service to build, train, deploy, and operate ML models (formerly Amazon SageMaker).

items.name: Studio, domains, and spaces
items.summary: A domain holds users and shared settings; JupyterLab and Code Editor spaces run on instances you choose.
items.details: You pay for the instances behind each running space. Idle shutdown stops apps after inactivity, which avoids paying for idle GPU notebooks.
items.example: GPU JupyterLab spaces that ran all weekend are stopped automatically by idle shutdown.
items.tip: Idle notebook costs → idle shutdown.

items.name: Execution roles
items.summary: Jobs, endpoints, and notebooks act with an IAM execution role; scope it to the buckets and keys they need.
items.details: Training jobs read data and write artifacts with the execution role. Reading SSE-KMS data also needs kms:Decrypt on the key.
items.example: A training job fails with AccessDenied until the role can decrypt the KMS key.

items.name: Instance quotas
items.summary: Each instance type has a per-account quota for training, endpoints, and notebooks, sometimes 0 by default.
items.details: ResourceLimitExceeded means the quota for that instance type is too low; request an increase in Service Quotas.
items.example: An ml.p4d.24xlarge training job fails until the quota is raised.

sections.title: SageMaker AI: data preparation and features
sections.summary: Data Wrangler in Canvas, processing jobs, and Feature Store.

items.name: Data Wrangler (in SageMaker Canvas)
items.summary: Visual data import, 300+ transforms, data quality and insights reports, and export to pipelines.
items.details: Data Wrangler now lives in SageMaker Canvas. Flows can be exported to processing jobs, SageMaker Pipelines, or Feature Store so the same transforms run in production. It includes a Balance data transform (random over/undersampling, SMOTE).
items.example: A flow built interactively runs weekly as part of a training pipeline.
items.tip: Reuse interactive transforms in production → export the Data Wrangler flow.

items.name: Processing jobs
items.summary: Run preprocessing, evaluation, or custom analysis scripts on managed, temporary instances.
items.details: Processing jobs use scikit-learn, Spark, or your own containers, read from S3, write results back, and stop when done.
items.example: A weekly processing job computes drift statistics on captured data.

items.name: Feature Store online and offline stores
items.summary: Online store: latest values in milliseconds for inference. Offline store: full history in S3 for training.
items.details: Feature groups need a record identifier and an event time. The offline store is registered in the Glue Data Catalog, so Athena can build point-in-time correct training sets.
items.example: Real-time fraud inference reads the latest card features; training joins historical features by event time.
items.tip: Avoid training/serving skew → the same feature definitions online and offline.

items.name: Feature Store ingestion
items.summary: PutRecord for streaming updates; batch ingestion from Spark, Data Wrangler, or processing jobs.
items.details: PutRecord writes to the online store immediately (and to the offline store when enabled). TTL can expire stale online records.
items.example: A Lambda function reading Kinesis calls PutRecord to update a 5-minute transaction count.

items.name: Ground Truth (legacy)
items.summary: Managed labeling with human workforces and automated labeling; closed to new customers since July 30, 2026.
items.details: Existing customers can still run labeling jobs with private or vendor workforces and active learning. Ground Truth Plus ended on June 30, 2026, and the Mechanical Turk workforce closed in September 2026. New projects use other labeling tools.
items.example: A team that already uses Ground Truth enables automated labeling to cut labeling cost.
items.tip: Know the concepts (workforces, consensus, active learning); expect the managed service only in “already uses” scenarios.

sections.title: SageMaker AI: training and tuning
sections.summary: Managed training jobs, built-in algorithms, script mode, distributed and spot training, and tuning.

items.name: Built-in algorithms
items.summary: XGBoost, Linear Learner, k-means, KNN, RCF, BlazingText, DeepAR, PCA, Factorization Machines, and more.
items.details: Built-in algorithms run from AWS containers with hyperparameters only. Learn what each is for: XGBoost/LightGBM/CatBoost (tabular), Linear Learner (interpretable linear), k-means (clustering), RCF (anomalies), BlazingText (text classification, Word2Vec), DeepAR (many related time series), Factorization Machines (sparse recommendations), IP Insights (unusual IP usage).
items.example: DeepAR forecasts 20,000 products by learning across related series.
items.tip: Match the data type and task to the algorithm.

items.name: Script mode and prebuilt containers
items.summary: Bring your own PyTorch, TensorFlow, Hugging Face, or scikit-learn script without building an image.
items.details: A framework estimator runs your entry-point script in an AWS Deep Learning Container. Extra packages go in requirements.txt in the source directory. Build your own container only when the prebuilt ones can’t work.
items.example: A laptop PyTorch script trains on GPU instances with the PyTorch estimator.
items.tip: Least effort for existing framework code → script mode.

items.name: Training input modes
items.summary: File mode downloads first; FastFile and Pipe stream from S3; FSx for Lustre and EFS are mountable.
items.details: Large datasets that delay job start benefit from FastFile mode. Repeated high-throughput reads benefit from FSx for Lustre linked to S3.
items.example: A job that spent 35 minutes downloading 2 TB starts at once with FastFile mode.

items.name: Managed spot training and checkpoints
items.summary: Up to 90% cheaper training on spare capacity; checkpoints to S3 let interrupted jobs resume.
items.details: Set use_spot_instances, a max_wait at least as long as max_run, and a checkpoint S3 URI.
items.example: A nightly 4-hour job runs on spot capacity and resumes from its last checkpoint after an interruption.
items.tip: Cheap, interruptible training → managed spot + checkpoints.

items.name: Managed warm pools
items.summary: Keep training instances provisioned after a job so the next matching job starts faster.
items.details: KeepAlivePeriodInSeconds keeps the cluster warm; useful for iterative experiments with many short jobs.
items.example: Back-to-back experiments skip several minutes of provisioning each.

items.name: Distributed training
items.summary: Data parallel when the model fits one GPU; sharded (FSDP) or model parallel when it doesn’t.
items.details: The SageMaker distributed data parallelism library speeds training on huge datasets. The model parallelism library (built on PyTorch FSDP) shards parameters, gradients, and optimizer states for very large models. Heterogeneous clusters mix CPU and GPU instance groups.
items.example: A 70B-parameter model trains with sharded data parallelism across many GPUs.
items.tip: Out of GPU memory at batch size 1 → shard the model, not more data parallelism.

items.name: SageMaker HyperPod and training plans
items.summary: Resilient clusters for large FM training with automatic node recovery; training plans reserve GPU capacity.
items.details: HyperPod (Slurm or EKS orchestration) replaces faulty nodes and resumes from checkpoints for long training runs. Training plans reserve accelerated capacity for a future time window.
items.example: A weeks-long pre-training run continues after a node failure without manual work.

items.name: Automatic model tuning (AMT)
items.summary: Bayesian (default), random, grid, or Hyperband search over hyperparameter ranges.
items.details: Define ranges (linear or logarithmic scaling) and an objective metric. Hyperband stops weak trials early and reallocates resources; early stopping type Auto ends unpromising Bayesian or random trials; warm start reuses earlier tuning jobs.
items.example: A tuning job with Hyperband explores 200 configurations within budget.
items.tip: Many expensive trials on a budget → Hyperband or early stopping.

items.name: SageMaker JumpStart
items.summary: Pretrained and foundation models to deploy or fine-tune in a few clicks, including PEFT methods.
items.details: JumpStart supports fine-tuning (including LoRA-style parameter-efficient methods) and deployment to SageMaker AI endpoints. Private curated hubs control which models teams can use.
items.example: A team fine-tunes an open-weight model with LoRA from JumpStart.

items.name: Debugger (legacy)
items.summary: Built-in rules for training problems such as vanishing gradients; closed to new customers since July 30, 2026.
items.details: AWS now recommends MLflow or TensorBoard on SageMaker for training metrics and model internals, and CloudWatch for system resource profiling. The Profiler feature is being retired.
items.example: A team that already uses Debugger gets an alert when its loss stops decreasing.
items.tip: Know the convergence problems; current tools are MLflow, TensorBoard, and CloudWatch.

sections.title: SageMaker AI: experiments, registry, and explainability
sections.summary: Managed MLflow, Model Registry, model cards, and SHAP-based explanations.

items.name: Managed MLflow on SageMaker AI
items.summary: Track parameters, metrics, and artifacts; compare runs; trace GenAI apps; register models.
items.details: MLflow runs as a tracking server or a serverless MLflow app. Models registered in MLflow can register automatically in SageMaker Model Registry and deploy with ModelBuilder.
items.example: Hundreds of tuning runs are compared in the MLflow UI and the best one is registered.
items.tip: Reproducible experiment tracking → MLflow (SageMaker Experiments in Studio Classic is the older option).

items.name: SageMaker Model Registry
items.summary: Model package groups, versions, metrics, lineage, and approval status for deployment and audits.
items.details: Statuses are PendingManualApproval, Approved, and Rejected. A status change emits an EventBridge event that can start deployment. IAM on UpdateModelPackage controls who can approve.
items.example: Only the risk team can approve models; approval starts the production deployment.
items.tip: Versioning, approval, and audit of models → Model Registry.

items.name: Model cards and lineage
items.summary: Document intended use, risk, and evaluation results; lineage tracks data, jobs, and models.
items.details: Model cards support governance reviews. Lineage tracking links datasets, training jobs, and deployed endpoints.
items.example: An auditor reviews a model card and the lineage graph for a credit model.

items.name: Clarify (legacy)
items.summary: Bias metrics and SHAP explanations; closed to new customers since July 30, 2026.
items.details: AWS’s replacement guidance: compute the same standardized bias metrics (CI, DPL, DI, and others) with pandas and scikit-learn, use the SHAP library directly, log results to MLflow, and use Bedrock Evaluations for foundation models.
items.example: A team without Clarify computes SHAP values in a processing step and logs them to MLflow.
items.tip: The metrics and SHAP concepts still matter; Clarify as a product is legacy.

sections.title: SageMaker AI: inference options
sections.summary: Real-time, serverless, asynchronous, and batch inference, plus multi-model hosting options.

items.name: Real-time endpoints
items.summary: Persistent, low-latency endpoints on chosen instances, including GPUs, with auto scaling.
items.details: Use for steady or latency-sensitive traffic. Two or more instances spread across Availability Zones for availability. Response streaming suits LLMs.
items.example: An interactive assistant serves an 8B model on a GPU endpoint.

items.name: Serverless Inference
items.summary: Scales to zero and bills per use; 1–6 GB memory, no GPUs, cold starts possible.
items.details: Good for intermittent traffic. Provisioned concurrency keeps capacity warm. It doesn’t support GPUs, VPC configuration, data capture, multiple variants, or multi-model endpoints.
items.example: A small model called a few hundred times a day costs almost nothing when idle.
items.tip: Spiky, infrequent, CPU-only traffic → serverless.

items.name: Asynchronous inference
items.summary: Queued requests with payloads up to 1 GB and processing up to 1 hour; can scale to zero.
items.details: Requests reference input in S3; results go to S3 with optional SNS notifications.
items.example: Video analysis jobs of 800 MB each finish in 20 minutes and notify the app.
items.tip: Large payloads or long processing → async inference.

items.name: Batch transform
items.summary: Score a whole dataset in S3 with no persistent endpoint.
items.details: Compute is released when the job ends; input can be split and processed in parallel.
items.example: Nightly churn scores for 40 million accounts.
items.tip: Whole dataset on a schedule → batch transform.

items.name: Multi-model, multi-container, and inference pipelines
items.summary: Share one endpoint across many models (same framework), up to 15 containers, or a chain of containers.
items.details: Multi-model endpoints load models from S3 on demand (thousands of small models). Multi-container endpoints host different frameworks with direct invocation. Inference pipelines run containers in sequence for one request.
items.example: 3,000 per-customer XGBoost models share one multi-model endpoint.

items.name: Inference components
items.summary: Several models on one endpoint, each with its own CPU/GPU/memory allocation and scaling.
items.details: Components scale copies per model (and can scale to zero), so FMs with different sizes share instances efficiently. Adapter inference components serve LoRA adapters on a shared base model.
items.example: Three fine-tuned models with different GPU needs share a fleet and scale independently.

items.name: Large model inference (LMI) containers
items.summary: Optimized serving (for example vLLM) with tensor parallelism across GPUs for big models.
items.details: Set the tensor parallel degree so a model larger than one GPU is sharded across the GPUs of an instance. The inference optimization toolkit adds techniques such as quantization and speculative decoding.
items.example: A 70B model loads across 8 GPUs with tensor parallel degree 8.

items.name: Inference Recommender
items.summary: Load tests across instance types to recommend cost-effective configurations for latency targets.
items.details: Use before launch to pick instance type and count.
items.example: It recommends two ml.c6i instances to meet 100 ms at 500 requests per second.

sections.title: SageMaker AI: scaling and safe releases
sections.summary: Auto scaling, deployment guardrails, shadow tests, and production variants.

items.name: Endpoint auto scaling
items.summary: Target tracking on InvocationsPerInstance, high-resolution concurrency metrics, or custom metrics such as GPU use.
items.details: Application Auto Scaling registers the variant (or inference component) as a scalable target. High-resolution ConcurrentRequestsPerModel and ConcurrentRequestsPerCopy emit every 10 seconds and react faster for long or streaming requests. Cooldowns control how quickly it scales in and out.
items.example: An LLM endpoint scales out quickly on concurrent requests instead of invocations per minute.
items.tip: Long-running or streaming requests → concurrency metrics; GPU-bound → GPUUtilization.

items.name: Deployment guardrails
items.summary: Blue/green (all at once, canary, linear) or rolling updates, with baking periods and alarm-based rollback.
items.details: Blue/green provisions a new fleet and shifts traffic; rolling updates replace capacity in batches, which avoids doubling an expensive fleet. CloudWatch alarms trigger automatic rollback.
items.example: 10% canary for 15 minutes, then full shift, rolling back if latency alarms fire.
items.tip: Small first step → canary; equal steps → linear; limited capacity → rolling.

items.name: Shadow tests
items.summary: A shadow variant gets a copy of live traffic, but its responses aren’t returned to callers.
items.details: Compare latency, errors, and predictions of a new model on real traffic with no customer impact, then promote it.
items.example: A new fraud model runs in shadow for a week before replacing production.
items.tip: No customer impact → shadow; measure business impact → A/B variants.

items.name: Production variants (A/B testing)
items.summary: Split live traffic between models by weight; TargetVariant routes a request to a named variant.
items.details: CloudWatch reports metrics per variant so business outcomes can be compared.
items.example: 90/10 split between the current and new model, with QA forcing requests to the new one.

sections.title: SageMaker AI: Pipelines and MLOps
sections.summary: SageMaker Pipelines workflows, step types, caching, and project templates.

items.name: Pipeline steps
items.summary: Processing, Training, Tuning, Model, RegisterModel, Transform, Condition, Fail, Lambda, Callback, and more.
items.details: A Condition step branches on metrics (for example register only if F1 ≥ 0.85, otherwise Fail). The @step decorator turns Python functions into steps. Pipelines record lineage.
items.example: A weekly pipeline processes data, trains, evaluates, and conditionally registers the model.
items.tip: Metric threshold gate → Condition step.

items.name: Step caching and triggers
items.summary: Reuse results of unchanged steps; start pipelines from EventBridge schedules or events.
items.details: Caching skips steps whose inputs and configuration haven’t changed. EventBridge can start a pipeline on a schedule or when a drift alarm fires.
items.example: A 2-hour processing step is skipped when its inputs haven’t changed.

items.name: SageMaker projects (MLOps templates)
items.summary: Templates that create source repositories, CI/CD pipelines, and deployment stages for ML.
items.details: Projects provision a standard build-train-deploy setup with CodePipeline and approval-based deployment.
items.example: A new team starts from a template that already has staging and production stages.

sections.title: SageMaker AI: monitoring (Model Monitor, legacy)
sections.summary: Data capture plus four monitor types; Model Monitor closed to new customers on July 30, 2026.

items.name: Data capture
items.summary: Record endpoint requests and responses (or batch transform inputs and outputs) to S3.
items.details: Captured data is the input for drift checks, whichever tool computes them. Keep disk use low so capture keeps working.
items.example: Captured requests are compared weekly with the training baseline.

items.name: Four monitoring types
items.summary: Data quality, model quality (needs ground truth), bias drift, and feature attribution drift.
items.details: Each compares production data with a baseline (statistics and constraints) on a schedule and reports violations to CloudWatch. Model quality needs labels joined to predictions.
items.example: Feature attribution drift catches a postcode feature suddenly dominating predictions.
items.tip: Know which type matches each symptom.

items.name: Current drift detection pattern
items.summary: Scheduled job computes drift (PSI, KS) on captured data, logs to MLflow, alarms in CloudWatch.
items.details: AWS’s replacement uses open-source tools (such as Evidently) in processing jobs or Lambda, MLflow for tracking, CloudWatch metrics with anomaly detection for alerts, and Quick Sight dashboards.
items.example: A weekly EventBridge-scheduled job publishes a drift score metric with an alarm.
items.tip: Drift detection pipeline = baseline + captured data + scheduled comparison + alarm.

sections.title: SageMaker AI: security
sections.summary: VPC configuration, network isolation, encryption, and IAM condition keys.

items.name: VPC and private connectivity
items.summary: Run jobs and endpoints in private subnets; use VPC endpoints for S3 and the SageMaker APIs.
items.details: An S3 gateway endpoint gives private subnets access to S3. Interface endpoints (PrivateLink) let applications call the SageMaker API and Runtime privately. Studio can run in VPC-only mode.
items.example: An endpoint in private subnets reads S3 through a gateway endpoint.

items.name: Network isolation
items.summary: The container gets no network access; SageMaker moves data in and out.
items.details: Use for untrusted third-party code or highly sensitive data. Inter-container traffic encryption protects data between distributed training nodes.
items.example: Third-party training code can’t send data anywhere.
items.tip: No outbound calls from the container → EnableNetworkIsolation.

items.name: Encryption with KMS
items.summary: KMS keys for training volumes, model artifacts, endpoint storage, and notebooks.
items.details: Use customer managed keys when the company must control and audit key use. AWS Config rules can flag endpoint configurations without a KMS key.
items.example: Every endpoint configuration must use a customer managed key.

items.name: IAM condition keys
items.summary: Enforce settings such as sagemaker:VpcSubnets, sagemaker:VolumeKmsKey, and sagemaker:NetworkIsolation.
items.details: Deny create calls unless the request uses approved subnets, keys, or isolation. Role Manager (legacy since July 2026) helped build persona-based roles.
items.example: CreateTrainingJob is denied unless the job uses the approved private subnets.
items.tip: Enforce SageMaker settings → IAM condition keys.

sections.title: Amazon Bedrock
sections.summary: Serverless access to foundation models from Amazon and other providers through one API.

items.name: Choosing a foundation model
items.summary: Compare models on task quality, context window, modalities, latency, price, and Region availability.
items.details: Use Bedrock evaluations on your own prompts to compare candidates objectively. Pick the smallest model that meets the quality bar to lower latency and cost.
items.example: Three models are compared on 500 claims with reference summaries before one is chosen.
items.tip: Objective model selection → evaluation jobs on your own data.

items.name: Converse and ConverseStream APIs
items.summary: One request format across models; streaming returns tokens as they are generated.
items.details: Inference parameters such as temperature, topP, and maxTokens control randomness and output length. The response includes a stopReason (for example end_turn or max_tokens) and token usage.
items.example: Streaming makes a chat assistant show its first words in a few hundred milliseconds.
items.tip: stopReason = max_tokens means the answer was cut off.

items.name: Bedrock Marketplace
items.summary: Discover 100+ specialized models and deploy them to managed SageMaker AI endpoints behind Bedrock APIs.
items.details: Marketplace models run on endpoints you size and pay for by instance, unlike serverless on-demand models.
items.example: A team deploys a domain-specific model from the Marketplace and calls it with the Converse API.

sections.title: Bedrock inference options and cost levers
sections.summary: On-demand tiers, cross-Region inference, Provisioned Throughput, batch, caching, and routing.

items.name: Service tiers
items.summary: Standard (default), Priority (faster, premium price), Flex (discount for slower processing), and Reserved capacity.
items.details: Set service_tier per request. Priority suits customer-facing work; Flex suits evaluations, summarization, and agent background work; Reserved (through the account team) reserves tokens-per-minute capacity for 1 or 3 months and overflows to Standard.
items.example: Nightly content tagging uses Flex; the live chat uses Standard or Priority.

items.name: Cross-Region inference
items.summary: Inference profiles route requests across Regions for throughput: geographic (data stays in a geography) or global.
items.details: Geographic profiles (for example US or EU) meet data residency needs at standard prices; global profiles route worldwide for about 10% savings. There’s no extra routing charge, and CloudTrail logs the Region that processed each request.
items.example: An EU company uses the EU geographic profile to absorb traffic peaks.
items.tip: Throttling plus residency rules → geographic profile; cost first → global.

items.name: Provisioned Throughput
items.summary: Dedicated model units for consistent, guaranteed capacity, with optional 1- or 6-month commitments.
items.details: Worth it for steady, high utilization; wasteful when traffic is low or spiky. Some customized models need it for inference.
items.example: A steady 24/7 workload with throttling buys model units; a low-traffic app stays on demand.

items.name: Batch inference
items.summary: Process large prompt sets from S3 asynchronously at a lower price than on-demand.
items.details: Submit JSONL records in S3; results are written back to S3. Use for offline jobs such as summarizing archives or generating evaluation data.
items.example: 2 million archived documents are summarized over two days at the batch price.
items.tip: Large offline jobs → batch inference.

items.name: Prompt caching
items.summary: Reuse a long repeated prompt prefix at a reduced price and with lower latency.
items.details: Mark cache checkpoints after stable content such as system prompts or reference documents. Cache writes can cost more, so it pays off when the prefix is reused.
items.example: A 30,000-token manual sent with every question is cached.
items.tip: Same long prefix on many calls → prompt caching.

items.name: Intelligent prompt routing
items.summary: A prompt router sends each request to the cheaper or the more capable model in a family.
items.details: The router predicts which model will answer each prompt well and chooses the cheaper one when possible.
items.example: Simple support questions go to the small model, hard ones to the large one.

items.name: Application inference profiles
items.summary: Tagged profiles that track usage and cost per application or team.
items.details: Applications invoke the profile instead of the model ID, and cost allocation tags split costs in Cost Explorer.
items.example: Three teams sharing one model see their own Bedrock costs.
items.tip: Bedrock cost per team or app → application inference profiles with tags.

sections.title: Bedrock model customization and import
sections.summary: Fine-tuning, reinforcement fine-tuning, distillation, continued pre-training, and Custom Model Import.

items.name: Supervised fine-tuning
items.summary: Labeled prompt and completion pairs in JSONL in S3 teach a task, format, or tone.
items.details: Training cost depends on tokens × epochs, plus monthly model storage. Supported custom models can be deployed for on-demand inference.
items.example: A bank fine-tunes a model on 8,000 approved letters to get a consistent format.
items.tip: Consistent style or task behavior from labeled examples → fine-tuning.

items.name: Reinforcement fine-tuning
items.summary: Improve a model with reward functions (for example Lambda graders) instead of labeled answers.
items.details: You supply prompts (or invocation logs) and a reward function that scores responses; the model learns from the scores.
items.example: A reward function checks that generated SQL runs and returns the expected rows.

items.name: Distillation
items.summary: A large teacher model generates responses to your prompts to train a smaller, cheaper student model.
items.details: Provide use-case prompts or invocation logs; labeled responses are optional.
items.example: A large model’s quality on ticket classification is transferred to a smaller, cheaper model.
items.tip: Smaller, cheaper model with similar quality, no labels → distillation.

items.name: Continued pre-training
items.summary: Adapt a model to a domain with large volumes of unlabeled text.
items.details: Use when you have plenty of domain documents but few labeled pairs. It’s offered for a limited set of models.
items.example: Millions of unlabeled research reports teach a model internal vocabulary.

items.name: Custom Model Import
items.summary: Bring open-weight models (for example Llama-architecture weights in Hugging Face format) into Bedrock.
items.details: Imported models are invoked serverlessly through the same Bedrock APIs, which is useful for models fine-tuned on another platform.
items.example: A model fine-tuned elsewhere is imported from S3 and called with the Bedrock API.
items.tip: Fine-tuned outside AWS, serve via Bedrock → Custom Model Import.

sections.title: Bedrock Knowledge Bases (managed RAG)
sections.summary: Ingest, chunk, embed, and retrieve your documents for grounded answers with citations.

items.name: Data sources, embeddings, and vector stores
items.summary: Choose data sources, an embedding model, and a vector store such as S3 Vectors, OpenSearch, or Aurora.
items.details: Supported stores include Amazon S3 Vectors, OpenSearch Serverless and managed clusters, Aurora PostgreSQL (pgvector), Neptune Analytics, and partner stores such as Pinecone. S3 Vectors is the lowest-cost option for large, rarely queried sets.
items.example: An HR knowledge base uses Titan Text Embeddings V2 and S3 Vectors.

items.name: Ingestion jobs (sync)
items.summary: A sync processes added, changed, and deleted documents incrementally.
items.details: Automate syncs after content changes (EventBridge schedule or Step Functions after ETL). Incremental syncs avoid re-embedding unchanged documents.
items.example: HR updates are searchable within the hour because a sync runs after each publish.
items.tip: Stale answers → run or automate ingestion jobs.

items.name: Parsing and chunking
items.summary: Advanced parsing (Bedrock Data Automation or an FM parser); chunking: fixed, hierarchical, semantic, none, or custom.
items.details: Hierarchical chunking returns parent context for precise child matches; semantic chunking splits on meaning; custom chunking uses a Lambda function. Metadata files add attributes for filtering.
items.example: Manuals with tables use advanced parsing and hierarchical chunks.

items.name: Retrieval configuration
items.summary: Hybrid or semantic search, number of results, metadata filters, reranking, and query decomposition.
items.details: Hybrid search helps with exact terms; filters restrict documents (for example by country); rerankers reorder candidates; decomposition splits multi-part questions.
items.example: German employees only retrieve German policies through a metadata filter.

items.name: Retrieve vs RetrieveAndGenerate
items.summary: Retrieve returns passages for your own prompt; RetrieveAndGenerate returns an answer with citations.
items.details: Use Retrieve when you need full control of prompt assembly or a different model; use RetrieveAndGenerate for the fastest managed RAG.
items.example: An app merges retrieved passages with user profile data before calling its chosen model.

sections.title: Bedrock Guardrails
sections.summary: Configurable safeguards for inputs and outputs, usable with any model through ApplyGuardrail.

items.name: Content filters and prompt attacks
items.summary: Hate, insults, sexual, violence, misconduct, and prompt attack filters with adjustable strength.
items.details: The prompt attack filter detects jailbreaks and prompt injection in tagged user input.
items.example: A message saying “ignore previous instructions” is blocked before it reaches the model.

items.name: Denied topics and word filters
items.summary: Block whole subject areas, profanity, or custom words and phrases.
items.details: Denied topics are described in natural language with examples.
items.example: A banking assistant refuses to give investment advice.

items.name: Sensitive information filters
items.summary: Detect PII types or regex patterns and block or mask them in inputs and outputs.
items.details: Masking replaces values with placeholders such as {PHONE} and still returns the rest of the response.
items.example: Customer phone numbers in answers are replaced with placeholders.
items.tip: Replace PII, keep the answer → mask; stop the response → block.

items.name: Contextual grounding and automated reasoning checks
items.summary: Flag responses not supported by the source or irrelevant to the query; verify facts against policies.
items.details: Grounding and relevance thresholds catch hallucinations in RAG. Automated Reasoning checks validate responses against formal rules derived from documents.
items.example: An answer that invents a refund period not in the policy is blocked.
items.tip: Hallucinations vs retrieved sources → contextual grounding check.

items.name: ApplyGuardrail API
items.summary: Evaluate any text against a guardrail without invoking a model.
items.details: Use it for self-hosted models, third-party models, or to screen data such as fine-tuning pairs.
items.example: Fine-tuning data is screened with ApplyGuardrail and flagged pairs are removed.

sections.title: Bedrock Evaluations
sections.summary: Evaluate models and RAG systems with programmatic metrics, judge models, or human workers.

items.name: Evaluation job types
items.summary: Programmatic (accuracy, robustness, toxicity), LLM-as-a-judge, human-based, and RAG evaluations.
items.details: You can use built-in or custom prompt datasets and bring your own responses from models outside Bedrock. Human jobs use your own work team for subjective judgments.
items.example: Legal experts rate two models’ answers for tone and soundness in a human evaluation job.

items.name: Judge-model metrics
items.summary: Correctness, completeness, faithfulness, helpfulness, coherence, relevance, plus harmfulness, stereotyping, and refusal.
items.details: An evaluator model scores each response and explains why. Custom metrics let you define your own rubric.
items.example: Weekly sampled production answers are scored for correctness and helpfulness.
items.tip: Scalable qualitative scoring → LLM-as-a-judge.

items.name: RAG evaluation
items.summary: Retrieve-only (context relevance and coverage) or retrieve-and-generate (correctness, faithfulness, citations).
items.details: Run retrieve-only first to isolate retrieval problems from generation problems.
items.example: Low context coverage shows that retrieval, not the model, causes wrong answers.

sections.title: Bedrock Prompt Management and Flows
sections.summary: Versioned prompts with variables and variants, and visual workflows that link prompts, models, and knowledge bases.

items.name: Prompt Management
items.summary: Store prompts with variables, test variants side by side, and create immutable versions.
items.details: Applications reference a prompt version ARN, so production stays on a tested prompt while drafts change.
items.example: Each tested prompt version is linked to its evaluation results.
items.tip: Reproducible prompt experiments and safe promotion → prompt versions.

items.name: Flows
items.summary: Visual workflows of prompts, models, knowledge bases, Lambda functions, and conditions, with versions and aliases.
items.details: Flows suit deterministic multi-step generative AI workflows without writing orchestration code.
items.example: A flow classifies a ticket, retrieves policies, and drafts a reply.

sections.title: Bedrock Agents Classic (legacy)
sections.summary: The original managed agents; closed to new customers on July 30, 2026. New work uses AgentCore.

items.name: Agents Classic
items.summary: Action groups, knowledge bases, versions and aliases; maintenance mode for existing customers.
items.details: Existing agents keep working with no planned end date, but new accounts can’t create them and newer models aren’t added. AWS recommends migrating to Bedrock AgentCore.
items.example: A team that already has a Classic agent pins production to an alias while it plans an AgentCore migration.
items.tip: Agents in new scenarios → AgentCore.

sections.title: Bedrock security, access, and logging
sections.summary: IAM, API keys, private connectivity, invocation logging, and data protection.

items.name: Data protection
items.summary: Prompts and responses aren’t used to train the base models or shared with model providers.
items.details: Data is encrypted in transit and at rest; customer managed KMS keys can encrypt custom models, knowledge bases, and other resources.
items.example: A healthcare company uses Bedrock knowing its prompts don’t train the shared models.

items.name: Bedrock API keys vs IAM credentials
items.summary: Short-term API keys (up to 12 hours) for exploration; long-term keys are tied to an IAM user; roles for production.
items.details: AWS recommends temporary IAM role credentials for production workloads (for example an ECS task role) and short-term API keys for quick experiments. Long-term keys should have expirations and rotation.
items.example: Hackathon developers use short-term keys; the production service uses its task role.
items.tip: Production → IAM roles; quick testing → short-term API keys.

items.name: IAM for models
items.summary: Allow bedrock:InvokeModel only on approved model or inference profile ARNs.
items.details: Resource-level permissions limit which models people and applications can call. SCPs can enforce this across accounts.
items.example: Developers can invoke only the two approved models.

items.name: Model invocation logging and private access
items.summary: Log prompts, responses, and token counts to CloudWatch Logs or S3; use VPC interface endpoints.
items.details: Invocation logging is off by default. CloudTrail records API calls; PrivateLink keeps traffic off the internet.
items.example: Every prompt and response is kept in S3 for audits.
items.tip: Record prompt and response content → invocation logging, not CloudTrail.

sections.title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
sections.summary: Modular services to deploy and operate agents built with any framework and any model.

items.name: Runtime
items.summary: Serverless hosting with per-session microVM isolation, long sessions (up to 8 hours), and MCP/A2A support.
items.details: Works with Strands Agents, LangGraph, CrewAI, or custom code. Consumption-based pricing; an Instances option runs on managed EC2 for multi-day or GPU workloads.
items.example: A Strands agent serves thousands of users with fully isolated sessions.
items.tip: Host an agent with session isolation and no servers → Runtime.

items.name: Versions and endpoints
items.summary: Every update creates an immutable version; DEFAULT tracks the latest; named endpoints pin a version.
items.details: Point production at a named endpoint and update it explicitly to promote or roll back.
items.example: PROD stays on version 3 while DEFAULT moves to version 4 for testing.

items.name: Gateway
items.summary: Turns OpenAPI, Smithy, and Lambda targets into MCP tools, with semantic tool search and inbound/outbound auth.
items.details: Gateway is a single secure entry point for tools, other agents, and model routing.
items.example: 40 internal APIs become MCP tools without custom integration code.
items.tip: Expose APIs as agent tools → Gateway.

items.name: Memory
items.summary: Short-term memory for turns within a session; long-term memory extracts preferences, facts, and summaries.
items.details: Long-term memory strategies run automatically across sessions so agents can personalize later conversations.
items.example: A travel agent remembers a user’s window-seat preference next month.

items.name: Identity
items.summary: Inbound authentication of users and outbound OAuth or API-key access to third-party services.
items.details: Identity stores and supplies per-user tokens so agent code never holds them.
items.example: An agent creates tickets in a SaaS tool on behalf of each signed-in user.

items.name: Observability
items.summary: OpenTelemetry traces of reasoning steps, tool calls, latency, and errors in CloudWatch.
items.details: Use it to find failing tools, loops, truncated outputs, and token-heavy sessions. It appears in CloudWatch generative AI observability.
items.example: Traces reveal one tool failing on 8% of calls.

items.name: Code Interpreter, Browser, Policy, and Evaluations
items.summary: Sandboxed code execution, web browsing, Cedar-based tool-call policies, and agent quality scoring.
items.details: Policy controls which tools an agent may call outside the agent code; Evaluations scores agent quality online and on demand.
items.example: Policy blocks a refund tool for amounts above a limit.

sections.title: Amazon Comprehend
sections.summary: NLP service: entities, sentiment, key phrases, language, PII, and custom classification and entities.

items.name: PII detection and redaction
items.summary: Find PII entities in text and produce redacted copies of documents in S3.
items.details: Useful before training on transcripts or tickets. Some features (topic modeling, event detection, prompt safety classification) closed to new customers in April 2026.
items.example: Call transcripts are redacted before fine-tuning.
items.tip: Redact PII in free text with least effort → Comprehend.

items.name: Custom classification and entity recognition
items.summary: Train classifiers or entity recognizers on your labeled text without ML expertise.
items.details: Needs labeled training data; good for domain-specific labels.
items.example: Support tickets are routed by a custom classifier.

sections.title: Amazon Comprehend Medical
sections.summary: Extract medical entities and protected health information (PHI) from clinical text.

items.name: Medical entities and ontology linking
items.summary: Detect medications, conditions, tests, and PHI; link to ICD-10-CM, RxNorm, and SNOMED CT.
items.details: No training required; HIPAA-eligible.
items.example: Clinical notes are coded to ICD-10-CM for analytics.
items.tip: Medical text with codes → Comprehend Medical.

sections.title: AWS HealthLake
sections.summary: HIPAA-eligible FHIR data store that normalizes and indexes health data for analytics and ML.

items.name: Health data in FHIR
items.summary: Store and query FHIR R4 resources, with integrated medical NLP and export for analytics.
items.details: HealthLake can enrich unstructured notes with medical entities and export data for Athena and SageMaker AI.
items.example: A hospital builds readmission features from FHIR data.

sections.title: Amazon Lex
sections.summary: Build voice and text chatbots with intents and slots; integrates with Lambda and Bedrock.

items.name: Conversational bots
items.summary: Intents capture what users want; slots collect required details.
items.details: Lex can use generative AI features, such as answering questions from a Bedrock knowledge base.
items.example: A booking bot collects dates and destination before calling a Lambda function.

sections.title: Amazon Personalize
sections.summary: Managed recommendations from interaction, item, and user data, with no ML expertise needed.

items.name: Recipes, campaigns, and events
items.summary: Choose a recipe, train a solution, serve it in a campaign or batch job, and stream new events.
items.details: An event tracker (PutEvents) updates recommendations as users click; filters apply business rules.
items.example: A startup adds personalized product recommendations without a data science team.
items.tip: Recommendations with the least ML expertise → Personalize.

sections.title: Amazon Polly
sections.summary: Text-to-speech with neural and generative voices, SSML, and custom lexicons.

items.name: Speech output
items.summary: Turn text into natural speech; SSML controls pronunciation, pauses, and emphasis.
items.details: Lexicons fix how brand names or acronyms are pronounced.
items.example: A product name is pronounced correctly through a custom lexicon.

sections.title: Amazon Rekognition
sections.summary: Image and video analysis: labels, faces, text, moderation, PPE, and Custom Labels.

items.name: Custom Labels
items.summary: Train detectors for your own objects or logos from a small labeled set.
items.details: Least-effort custom computer vision without ML expertise. Streaming video events and batch image content moderation closed to new customers in April 2026.
items.example: 200 labeled images train a logo detector.
items.tip: Company-specific objects → Custom Labels.

sections.title: Amazon Textract
sections.summary: Extract text, forms, tables, and fields from documents, with specialized APIs.

items.name: Document APIs
items.summary: AnalyzeDocument (forms, tables, queries), AnalyzeExpense (invoices, receipts), AnalyzeID, and more.
items.details: No training required. Queries ask for specific fields in natural language.
items.example: Vendor names and totals are extracted from scanned invoices.
items.tip: Invoices and receipts → AnalyzeExpense.

sections.title: Amazon Transcribe
sections.summary: Speech to text with custom vocabularies and language models, diarization, PII redaction, and streaming.

items.name: Transcription features
items.summary: Custom vocabulary for terms, speaker diarization, PII redaction, Call Analytics, and Medical.
items.details: Transcribe output often feeds NLP pipelines for training or analytics.
items.example: Call recordings are transcribed with PII redacted before analysis.

sections.title: Amazon Translate
sections.summary: Neural machine translation, real-time or batch, with custom terminology.

items.name: Translation and augmentation
items.summary: Translate content in real time or in batch; back-translation also creates paraphrases for data augmentation.
items.details: Custom terminology keeps brand and product names consistent.
items.example: Back-translation adds variety to a small intent dataset.

sections.title: Amazon CodeGuru (legacy)
sections.summary: Code reviews and profiling; Reviewer closed to new customers in November 2025 and Security was discontinued.

items.name: What remains
items.summary: CodeGuru Profiler finds expensive code paths at run time; for code security AWS points to Amazon Inspector.
items.details: The exam guide still names CodeGuru for securing CI/CD. For new setups, Amazon Inspector scans code, dependencies, and images.
items.example: A team without CodeGuru Reviewer uses Inspector code scanning in its pipeline.
items.tip: Code and image vulnerabilities today → Amazon Inspector.

sections.title: Amazon DevOps Guru (legacy)
sections.summary: ML-powered detection of operational anomalies; entering sunset with end of support on September 30, 2027.

items.name: Operational insights
items.summary: Analyzes metrics, logs, and events to flag anomalous behavior and suggest fixes.
items.details: For new setups, CloudWatch anomaly detection and Application Signals cover similar needs.
items.example: DevOps Guru flags rising latency in an inference API before users complain.

sections.title: AWS Auto Scaling
sections.summary: Scaling for AWS resources; Application Auto Scaling scales SageMaker endpoints and inference components.

items.name: Application Auto Scaling for endpoints
items.summary: Register a variant or inference component as a scalable target, then add target tracking, step, or scheduled policies.
items.details: Set minimum and maximum capacity and cooldowns. Scheduled scaling handles known peaks; target tracking follows a metric.
items.example: An endpoint scales from 2 to 10 instances on invocations per instance and pre-scales before a daily batch of traffic.

sections.title: AWS CloudFormation
sections.summary: Infrastructure as code with templates, stacks, change sets, and cross-stack references.

items.name: Repeatable ML infrastructure
items.summary: Define endpoints, roles, buckets, and pipelines as code and deploy them the same way in every account.
items.details: Outputs with Export and Fn::ImportValue share values such as subnet IDs between stacks. Change sets preview updates; stack rollback undoes failed changes.
items.example: Endpoint stacks import the VPC and subnets exported by a networking stack.
items.tip: Share values between stacks → Export + Fn::ImportValue.

sections.title: AWS CloudTrail
sections.summary: Records API activity: who did what, when, and from where.

items.name: Auditing ML resources
items.summary: Management events record calls such as CreateEndpoint and UpdateModelPackage; data events are opt-in.
items.details: CloudTrail shows the identity, time, and source IP of each call. It doesn’t record prompt or response content; use Bedrock invocation logging for that.
items.example: An auditor finds who updated a production endpoint last Tuesday.
items.tip: Who changed what → CloudTrail.

sections.title: Amazon CloudWatch
sections.summary: Metrics, logs, alarms, dashboards, anomaly detection, and generative AI observability.

items.name: Endpoint and model metrics
items.summary: Invocations, ModelLatency, OverheadLatency, 4XX/5XX errors, and CPU, memory, and GPU utilization.
items.details: ModelLatency is time inside the container; OverheadLatency is SageMaker’s added time. Bedrock publishes invocations, latency, token counts, and throttles.
items.example: Comparing ModelLatency and OverheadLatency shows the model itself slowed down.

items.name: Alarms and anomaly detection
items.summary: Alarm on thresholds, or let anomaly detection learn normal patterns including weekly seasonality.
items.details: Publish custom metrics (record counts, drift scores, share of truncated responses) and alarm on them.
items.example: A low daily record count triggers an anomaly alarm without a fixed threshold.
items.tip: Values that vary by weekday → anomaly detection alarm.

items.name: Generative AI observability
items.summary: Prebuilt dashboards for model invocations and AgentCore agents: latency, tokens, errors, and traces.
items.details: Generally available since October 2025; works with agents built with frameworks such as Strands and LangGraph.
items.example: Operations sees token usage and error rates per model on one page.

items.name: Dashboards and Logs Insights
items.summary: Combine metrics and alarms on one screen; query logs interactively.
items.details: Logs Insights can search invocation logs, for example for responses with stopReason max_tokens.
items.example: An MLOps dashboard shows endpoint latency, Bedrock tokens, and pipeline failures.

sections.title: AWS Compute Optimizer
