sections.summary: Rightsizing recommendations from utilization history for EC2, EBS, Lambda, ECS on Fargate, and more.

items.name: Rightsizing
items.summary: Find over-provisioned instances and functions behind ML applications.
items.details: It analyzes CloudWatch metrics and recommends better-sized or cheaper options. For SageMaker AI endpoints, use Inference Recommender and endpoint metrics instead.
items.example: An oversized EC2 preprocessing fleet is downsized.

sections.title: AWS Config
sections.summary: Records resource configurations and evaluates them against rules continuously.

items.name: Compliance rules for ML resources
items.summary: Managed rules flag, for example, endpoint configurations without a KMS key or notebooks with direct internet access.
items.details: Config detects drift from policy after resources exist; IAM conditions prevent noncompliant creation up front.
items.example: A rule flags any endpoint configuration that lacks a customer managed key.
items.tip: Continuous detection → Config; prevention → IAM conditions or SCPs.

sections.title: AWS Organizations
sections.summary: Manage multiple accounts with consolidated billing and service control policies (SCPs).

items.name: Multi-account guardrails
items.summary: Separate dev, staging, and production ML accounts; SCPs restrict actions such as using unapproved Regions or models.
items.details: SCPs set the maximum permissions in member accounts; they don’t grant access.
items.example: An SCP denies Bedrock calls outside approved Regions for every account.

sections.title: AWS Service Catalog
sections.summary: Publish approved, pre-configured products that teams launch in self-service.

items.name: Approved ML environments
items.summary: Offer vetted templates (for example a secure notebook or endpoint) so teams provision compliant resources.
items.details: SageMaker projects use Service Catalog products for MLOps templates.
items.example: Data scientists launch a pre-approved, encrypted training environment.

sections.title: AWS Systems Manager
sections.summary: Operations hub: Parameter Store, Session Manager, patching, and automation.

items.name: Parameter Store
items.summary: Store configuration values and simple secrets; use Secrets Manager when you need rotation.
items.details: Pipelines read settings such as model thresholds or endpoint names from Parameter Store.
items.example: A deployment pipeline reads the approved instance type from a parameter.

sections.title: AWS Trusted Advisor
sections.summary: Best-practice checks for cost, security, fault tolerance, performance, and service quotas.

items.name: Account-level checks
items.summary: Flags issues such as idle resources, open security groups, and quotas nearing limits.
items.details: Useful as a general review; it doesn’t provide model or invocation dashboards.
items.example: A check warns that an instance quota is close to its limit.

sections.title: Amazon Kinesis Video Streams
sections.summary: Securely stream live video from devices to AWS for storage, playback, and ML.

items.name: Live video ingestion
items.summary: Ingest camera streams for computer vision models and replay them later.
items.details: Consumers (for example a SageMaker AI endpoint or custom application) read frames for near-real-time inference.
items.example: Factory cameras stream video so a model can detect safety violations.
items.tip: Live video for ML → Kinesis Video Streams.

sections.title: AWS DataSync
sections.summary: Automated, encrypted online transfer from NFS, SMB, HDFS, or other clouds to S3, EFS, or FSx.

items.name: Moving datasets to AWS
items.summary: Copy large on-premises datasets with integrity checks, scheduling, and bandwidth limits.
items.details: DataSync handles bulk or recurring transfers; Storage Gateway gives ongoing hybrid access.
items.example: 80 TB of labeled images move from an NFS server to S3 once.
items.tip: One-time or scheduled bulk transfer → DataSync.

sections.title: Amazon API Gateway
sections.summary: Managed front door for REST, HTTP, and WebSocket APIs with auth, throttling, and caching.

items.name: Exposing models as APIs
items.summary: Put an API in front of Lambda or SageMaker endpoints with authentication and usage plans.
items.details: API Gateway adds throttling, API keys for partners, and request validation; it doesn’t turn APIs into agent tools (AgentCore Gateway does).
items.example: Partners call a scoring API with keys and rate limits.

sections.title: Amazon CloudFront
sections.summary: Global content delivery network with edge caching and security integrations.

items.name: Global delivery for AI apps
items.summary: Serve web front ends and cacheable responses close to users.
items.details: Not a model hosting service; it accelerates and protects the application layer.
items.example: A chatbot’s web front end is served globally from edge locations.

sections.title: AWS Direct Connect
sections.summary: Dedicated private network connection from on premises to AWS.

items.name: Consistent hybrid bandwidth
items.summary: Move large datasets or reach endpoints privately with predictable throughput.
items.details: Often combined with DataSync for large recurring transfers.
items.example: A bank sends nightly training extracts to S3 over Direct Connect.

sections.title: Amazon VPC
sections.summary: Isolated networks with subnets, security groups, route tables, and VPC endpoints.

items.name: Isolating ML workloads
items.summary: Private subnets plus security groups for jobs, endpoints, and Studio; no internet path unless you add one.
items.details: Gateway endpoints (S3, DynamoDB) and interface endpoints (SageMaker API and Runtime, Bedrock, CloudWatch) keep traffic on the AWS network.
items.example: An endpoint and its callers communicate only inside the VPC.
items.tip: Private access to AWS services → VPC endpoints, not NAT or internet gateways.

sections.title: AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM)
sections.summary: Users, roles, and policies that control access to every AWS resource.

items.name: Least privilege for ML
items.summary: Scope execution roles to the needed actions and S3 prefixes; separate who trains, approves, and deploys.
items.details: Avoid broad managed policies such as AmazonS3FullAccess for jobs. Deny UpdateModelPackage to data scientists to separate duties.
items.example: A training role can read only s3://ml-data/fraud/ and write only s3://ml-artifacts/fraud/.

items.name: Condition keys
items.summary: Allow or deny based on request values such as subnets, KMS keys, or model ARNs.
items.details: Combine with SCPs for organization-wide guardrails.
items.example: Training jobs are denied unless they use approved subnets and a KMS key.

sections.title: Amazon Inspector
sections.summary: Continuous vulnerability scanning for EC2, ECR container images, and Lambda functions and code.

items.name: Container image scanning
items.summary: Finds CVEs in OS and language packages in ECR images, on push and continuously.
items.details: Findings go to EventBridge and Security Hub, so pipelines can block images with critical vulnerabilities. Inspector also integrates with CI/CD tools to scan during builds.
items.example: A deployment stage fails when a new inference image has a critical CVE.
items.tip: Vulnerabilities in images or dependencies → Inspector.

items.name: Lambda code scanning
items.summary: Scans Lambda dependencies and function code for issues such as injection flaws and hard-coded secrets.
items.details: This is AWS’s recommended path for code security now that CodeGuru Reviewer and CodeGuru Security are closed.
items.example: A tool function that builds SQL from user input is flagged for injection.

sections.title: AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS)
sections.summary: Create and control encryption keys; every use is logged in CloudTrail.

items.name: Customer managed keys
items.summary: Encrypt training data, artifacts, volumes, knowledge bases, and custom models with keys you control.
items.details: Access needs both an IAM permission and a key policy that allows it; a missing kms:Decrypt causes AccessDenied when reading SSE-KMS data.
items.example: A training job can read encrypted data once its role is allowed to use the key.
items.tip: AccessDenied on SSE-KMS objects → check kms:Decrypt.

sections.title: Amazon Macie
sections.summary: Discovers sensitive data such as PII in Amazon S3 with ML and pattern matching.

items.name: Finding PII in training data
items.summary: Scan buckets to learn where sensitive data lives before it is used for training.
items.details: Macie reports findings; masking or redaction happens elsewhere (Glue, Comprehend, Guardrails).
items.example: Macie shows that two of 40 buckets hold customer phone numbers.
items.tip: Where is the PII in S3? → Macie.

sections.title: AWS Secrets Manager
sections.summary: Store, control access to, and automatically rotate secrets such as API keys and passwords.

items.name: Secrets for jobs and agents
items.summary: Jobs and functions read secrets at run time with their role; nothing is stored in code or images.
items.details: Rotation can run automatically; hyperparameters and environment variables baked into images are visible to others.
items.example: A processing job fetches a partner API key from Secrets Manager at start-up.

sections.title: Amazon EBS
sections.summary: Block storage volumes for EC2 and for SageMaker AI training and notebook instances.

items.name: Instance volumes
items.summary: Per-instance storage that can be encrypted with KMS; not shared across many instances.
items.details: SageMaker AI attaches ML storage volumes to training instances; specify a KMS key to encrypt them.
items.example: Training volumes are encrypted with the company’s key.

sections.title: Amazon EFS
sections.summary: Elastic, shared POSIX file system that many instances can mount at once.

items.name: Shared files for teams
items.summary: Share code, libraries, and intermediate data across Studio and EC2.
items.details: Elastic throughput suits spiky access; for sustained high-throughput training reads, FSx for Lustre is usually faster.
items.example: Data scientists share a 200 GB feature cache across notebooks.

sections.title: Amazon FSx
sections.summary: Managed file systems, including FSx for Lustre for high-performance ML training.

items.name: FSx for Lustre linked to S3
items.summary: Parallel, high-throughput access to training data that lazy-loads from and syncs with S3.
items.details: Keeps GPUs busy when many epochs read terabytes of data.
items.example: A 40 TB image dataset is read at full speed every epoch.
items.tip: GPU starvation on large S3 datasets → FSx for Lustre.

sections.title: Amazon S3
sections.summary: Object storage for datasets, artifacts, logs, and vectors (S3 Vectors).

items.name: The ML data lake
items.summary: Durable, scalable storage for raw and curated data, model artifacts, and captured inference data.
items.details: Organize by prefix and partition; prefer large columnar files over millions of tiny objects; encrypt with SSE-KMS when keys must be customer-controlled.
items.example: Training data, model.tar.gz artifacts, and endpoint data capture all live in S3.

items.name: Amazon S3 Vectors
items.summary: Purpose-built, serverless vector buckets and indexes with sub-second queries at low cost.
items.details: Best for large, infrequently queried vector sets; integrates with Bedrock knowledge bases and OpenSearch.
items.example: A legal archive of 400 million chunks is searchable for a fraction of a cluster’s cost.
items.tip: Cheapest vector storage at scale → S3 Vectors.

sections.title: Amazon S3 Glacier storage classes
sections.summary: Low-cost archive storage classes for data you rarely access.

items.name: Archiving datasets and artifacts
items.summary: Instant Retrieval, Flexible Retrieval, and Deep Archive trade access speed for cost.
items.details: Lifecycle rules move old training data or logs to Glacier classes. Data in Flexible Retrieval or Deep Archive must be restored before jobs can read it. (The older vault-based Amazon Glacier service closed to new customers in 2025.)
items.example: Raw data older than a year moves to Deep Archive automatically.

sections.title: AWS Storage Gateway
sections.summary: Hybrid storage that gives on-premises applications access to cloud storage.

items.name: Ongoing hybrid access
items.summary: S3 File Gateway presents S3 as NFS or SMB shares on premises.
items.details: Use it when on-premises tools keep writing data that should land in S3; use DataSync for bulk transfers.
items.example: Lab instruments write images to a file share that is backed by S3.

sections.group: Domain 1 · Data preparation for ML and AI
sections.title: Collect and store data
sections.summary: Task 1.1: sources, formats, storage choices, streaming, merging, vector stores, and features.

items.name: Data formats and access patterns
items.summary: Columnar (Parquet, ORC) for analytics; row formats (CSV, JSON) for interchange; JSONL for LLM data.
items.details: Columnar formats read only the needed columns and compress well, so they suit training extracts and Athena. CSV and JSON are simple but larger and slower. RecordIO-protobuf is used by some built-in algorithms. JSON Lines is the usual format for prompts and fine-tuning data.
items.example: Converting 3 years of CSV to Parquet cuts Athena scans by over 80%.
items.tip: Analytics on a few columns → Parquet/ORC.

items.name: Choosing storage for ML
items.summary: S3 for the data lake; FSx for Lustre for fast training reads; EFS for shared files; EBS per instance.
items.details: Decide by cost, throughput, sharing, data structure, and compliance (encryption with customer managed keys, retention, residency).
items.example: GPU instances waiting on data → FSx for Lustre linked to the S3 bucket.

items.name: Ingestion capacity problems
items.summary: Hot shards, small files, throttling, long downloads, and out-of-memory ETL jobs.
items.details: Fixes: high-cardinality partition keys or on-demand streams; compacting small files; FastFile mode; bigger or more Glue workers and job bookmarks; retries with backoff for throttling.
items.example: Hot shard → device ID as the partition key.

items.name: Streaming ingestion choices
items.summary: Kinesis Data Streams (custom consumers), Data Firehose (delivery), Flink (stateful processing), Apache Kafka.
items.details: Data Streams for millisecond custom processing; Firehose to deliver to S3/Redshift/OpenSearch with format conversion; Managed Service for Apache Flink for windows and joins; Kafka-based sources can feed the same pipelines.
items.example: Clickstream to Parquet in S3 → Firehose; rolling 15-minute counts → Flink.

items.name: Merging sources
items.summary: Join databases, files, and streams with Glue ETL or Spark; broadcast small tables.
items.details: Glue connects to JDBC sources and S3; Spark broadcast joins avoid shuffling a huge table; deduplicate keys before joining.
items.example: A nightly Glue job joins RDS customers with S3 purchases.

items.name: Choosing a vector store
items.summary: OpenSearch (fast, hybrid), pgvector (beside SQL data), S3 Vectors (cheapest at scale), Neptune Analytics (GraphRAG).
items.details: Match to latency, query volume, scale, existing databases, filtering needs, and cost. Index types such as HNSW trade memory for speed and recall.
items.example: An archive of 400 million chunks queried rarely → S3 Vectors.

items.name: Storing diverse data types
items.summary: Keep images, audio, and video in S3 with a metadata index; stream live video with Kinesis Video Streams.
items.details: Metadata (labels, durations, consent flags) in a table or catalog makes datasets easy to filter and assemble.
items.example: Podcast audio and cover images in S3, with episode metadata in DynamoDB.

items.name: Feature Store ingestion
items.summary: Stream with PutRecord; batch-ingest historical data; use event time for point-in-time joins.
items.details: The same feature definitions online and offline prevent training/serving skew.
items.example: A 5-minute transaction count is streamed to the online store.

sections.group: Domain 1 · Data preparation for ML and AI
sections.title: Transform data and engineer features
sections.summary: Task 1.2: tools, feature engineering, embeddings, text prep, RAG documents, masking, and FM data.

items.name: Picking a transformation tool
items.summary: Glue (serverless ETL), DataBrew (no-code), Data Wrangler (ML-focused, visual), EMR (big Spark), Lambda (streams).
items.details: Choose by user skills, data size, need for code control, and whether the transform must run in a pipeline.
items.example: Analysts without code → DataBrew; existing PySpark → EMR.

items.name: Scaling numeric features
items.summary: Standardization (mean 0, std 1) or min-max normalization (0–1) for distance- and gradient-based models.
items.details: KNN, k-means, SVMs, linear models, and neural networks are sensitive to scale; tree models are not. Fit scalers on training data only.
items.example: Income in millions dominates age until both are standardized.
items.tip: Distance-based model ignoring a feature → scale features.

items.name: Log transforms, binning, and splitting
items.summary: Log for right-skewed values; binning for stage-like effects; split timestamps into parts.
items.details: Feature splitting extracts hour, day of week, or domain from a URL. Binning creates ordered groups.
items.example: Order timestamps become hour-of-day and day-of-week features.

items.name: Encoding categories
items.summary: One-hot for few nominal values; ordinal for ordered values; target or hashing for high cardinality.
items.details: Label/ordinal codes imply order and distance. One-hot explodes with thousands of values, where target encoding or feature hashing scale better.
items.example: Five payment methods → one-hot; 50,000 merchant IDs → target encoding or hashing.

items.name: Transforming streaming data
items.summary: Stateless per-record logic in Lambda or Firehose transforms; stateful windows in Flink or Spark.
items.details: Keep stream transforms idempotent and handle retries.
items.example: Fahrenheit to Celsius conversion in a Lambda consumer.

items.name: Embeddings
items.summary: Dense vectors that capture meaning; use the same model for documents and queries.
items.details: Choose by modality (text or multimodal), language support, dimensions, and cost. Fewer dimensions cut storage with some accuracy loss; normalization enables cosine similarity.
items.example: Titan Text Embeddings V2 at 512 dimensions halves vector storage with little recall loss.
items.tip: Changing the embedding model means re-embedding everything.

items.name: Text pre-processing and tokenization
items.summary: Tokenize with the model’s own tokenizer; augment small datasets with back-translation or paraphrases.
items.details: Subword tokenizers split rare words into pieces. Classic NLP steps (lowercasing, stop words, stemming) matter more for simple models than for LLMs.
items.example: A dataset pre-tokenized for another model is re-tokenized with the base model’s tokenizer.

items.name: Preparing documents for RAG
items.summary: Parse complex files, pick a chunking strategy and overlap, and attach metadata for filtering.
items.details: Fixed-size chunking is simple; hierarchical keeps parent context; semantic follows meaning; no chunking suits short, self-contained docs. Metadata such as country, date, or product enables filters.
items.example: Policies tagged with country let retrieval filter by the employee’s location.

items.name: Masking, redaction, and anonymization
items.summary: Redact (remove), mask (replace), hash or tokenize (consistent pseudonyms), or generalize values.
items.details: Hashing keeps joins possible without exposing raw values. Anonymized data shouldn’t be re-identifiable; pseudonymized data can be with the key.
items.example: Emails are hashed so the same customer still links across tables.

items.name: Data for FM customization
items.summary: Fine-tuning: labeled prompt/completion pairs. Continued pre-training: unlabeled text. Distillation: prompts.
items.details: Reinforcement fine-tuning needs prompts plus a reward function. Hold out a validation set and keep the format consistent (JSONL in S3).
items.example: 5,000 spec-to-description pairs fine-tune a model for product copy.

sections.group: Domain 1 · Data preparation for ML and AI
sections.title: Validate data quality and manage bias
sections.summary: Task 1.3: quality checks, labeling, splits, bias metrics, imbalance, data integrity, and cleaning.

items.name: Data quality dimensions
items.summary: Completeness, uniqueness, validity, consistency, accuracy, and timeliness.
items.details: Automate checks in pipelines (Glue Data Quality, DataBrew rules) and fail fast before bad data reaches training.
items.example: A rule fails the job when a key column is 40% null.

items.name: Labeling and annotation strategies
items.summary: Human labelers with consensus, active learning, LLM-assisted pre-labeling with human review.
items.details: Clear instructions, multiple annotators per item, and audits keep labels consistent. Active learning sends only uncertain items to humans. (SageMaker Ground Truth is legacy for new customers.)
items.example: An LLM pre-labels tickets and humans review only low-confidence ones.

items.name: Splitting and shuffling
items.summary: Random, stratified (keeps class ratios), time-based (no future data), and group-based splits.
items.details: Shuffle independent rows; never shuffle across time for forecasting. Keep all rows of one entity (customer, patient) in one split.
items.example: A rare-disease dataset uses a stratified split so validation contains positives.

items.name: Bias metrics
items.summary: Pre-training: class imbalance (CI), difference in proportions of labels (DPL). Post-training: DI, DPPL.
items.details: Pre-training metrics describe the data; post-training metrics compare predictions between groups (facets). Other measures include KL and JS divergence of label distributions.
items.example: CI shows applicants over 60 are underrepresented; DPL shows their approval rate differs.
items.tip: Know which metrics are pre- vs post-training.

items.name: Bias across numeric, text, and image data
items.summary: Measure group representation and outcomes in every modality before training.
items.details: For images, label sensitive attributes for audit; for text, check dialects and topics; rebalance or collect data where groups are thin.
items.example: Skin tones and age groups are counted before training a face model.

items.name: Class imbalance
items.summary: Resample (oversample, undersample, SMOTE), weight classes, augment, and use precision/recall, not accuracy.
items.details: Resample only the training data; keep validation and test sets at the real distribution.
items.example: 0.3% fraud → SMOTE on training data and PR-AUC for evaluation.

items.name: AI training data integrity
items.summary: Validate prompt-response pairs, deduplicate, screen for unsafe content and PII, and protect evaluation sets.
items.details: Check schemas, remove empty or truncated pairs, screen with ApplyGuardrail, and make sure test items don’t leak into training.
items.example: Offensive pairs are removed from 20,000 employee-written examples before fine-tuning.

items.name: Cleaning: outliers, missing values, duplicates
items.summary: Detect outliers (IQR, z-scores, Random Cut Forest), impute (median, mode, model-based), deduplicate.
items.details: Add a missing-value indicator when missingness carries signal. Deduplicate before splitting to avoid leakage.
items.example: Median income plus an “imputed” flag replaces 8% missing values.

items.name: Data leakage
items.summary: Features or splits that reveal the label or future information inflate validation scores.
items.details: Remove features created after the outcome; split before fitting scalers and encoders; keep time order.
items.example: cancellation_reason is dropped from a churn model.
items.tip: Suspiciously good validation → look for leakage.

sections.group: Domain 2 · ML model and FM development
sections.title: Choose a modeling approach
sections.summary: Task 2.1: FM selection, customization strategy, algorithms, managed services, RAG patterns, trade-offs.

items.name: Framing the ML problem
items.summary: Classification, regression, clustering, forecasting, anomaly detection, recommendation, NLP, vision, generation.
items.details: Start by asking whether ML is needed and what output the business uses; then pick the simplest approach that meets the requirement.
items.example: Predicting next week’s demand per product is a forecasting problem, not classification.

items.name: Algorithm fit
items.summary: Trees (XGBoost) for tabular; linear for interpretability; CNNs and ViTs for images; transformers for text.
items.details: Deep learning shines with unstructured data; gradient-boosted trees usually win on tabular data at low cost.
items.example: Tabular churn data → XGBoost on CPUs.

items.name: Selecting a foundation model
items.summary: Modality, context window, quality on your data, latency, price, customization support, Region, and license.
items.details: Evaluate on your own prompts rather than general leaderboards.
items.example: A smaller model matches a large one on short support questions and halves latency.

items.name: The customization ladder
items.summary: Prompt engineering → RAG → fine-tuning → continued pre-training → training from scratch.
items.details: Each step adds cost and complexity. RAG adds current knowledge with citations; fine-tuning changes behavior, style, and format; pre-training adapts to a domain’s language.
items.example: Fast-changing product facts → RAG; consistent letter format → fine-tuning.
items.tip: Choose the cheapest step that meets the requirement.

items.name: Fine-tuning strategies
items.summary: Full fine-tuning vs parameter-efficient methods (LoRA, adapters); instruction tuning; domain adaptation.
items.details: PEFT trains a small number of extra weights, needs less GPU memory, keeps per-task artifacts small, and reduces catastrophic forgetting.
items.example: Three LoRA adapters share one frozen 13B base model.

items.name: Managed service, pre-trained model, or custom
items.summary: AI services for common tasks; FMs for flexible language tasks; custom models for unique data and needs.
items.details: Least effort usually means an AI service (Textract, Comprehend, Rekognition, Personalize) when it fits the task.
items.example: Invoice fields → Textract AnalyzeExpense instead of training a model.

items.name: RAG architecture patterns
items.summary: Vector RAG, hybrid search, reranking, query decomposition, hierarchical chunks, GraphRAG, NL-to-SQL, agentic RAG.
items.details: Pick by question type: exact identifiers → hybrid; multi-hop relationships → GraphRAG; numbers in tables → structured retrieval; multi-step tasks → agents.
items.example: Revenue questions over Redshift use structured retrieval, not embeddings.

items.name: Performance vs training time vs cost
items.summary: Simpler models, sampled data, spot capacity, early stopping, and distributed training change the balance.
items.details: A slightly less accurate model that trains in minutes may be the right business choice.
items.example: XGBoost reaches 98% of a deep model’s accuracy at a tenth of the cost.

items.name: Quality vs latency vs cost for FMs
items.summary: Model size, prompt length, output length, caching, routing, distillation, and service tier.
items.details: Larger models are slower and costlier per token; distillation and routing keep quality where it matters.
items.example: A cascade sends 85% of tickets to a small model.

sections.group: Domain 2 · ML model and FM development
sections.title: Train, fine-tune, and customize models
sections.summary: Task 2.2: training settings, tuning, faster training, fitting problems, ensembles, prompts, retrieval.

items.name: Core hyperparameters
items.summary: Epochs, batch size, learning rate, steps, and model-specific settings such as max_depth.
items.details: Too high a learning rate oscillates or diverges; too low is slow. Larger batches are faster per epoch but may generalize differently.
items.example: Loss jumping up and down → lower the learning rate.

items.name: Hyperparameter optimization
items.summary: Search ranges with log scaling for rates; Bayesian, random, grid, or Hyperband; objective metric.
items.details: Use logarithmic scaling for ranges that span orders of magnitude (for example 0.0001–0.1).
items.example: Hyperband stops weak trials early in a large deep learning search.

items.name: Reducing training time
items.summary: Early stopping, distributed training, better input modes, mixed precision, warm pools, and smaller models.
items.details: Measure where time goes: data loading, compute, or waiting for capacity.
items.example: FastFile mode plus early stopping cut a 6-hour job to 2 hours.

items.name: Overfitting and underfitting
items.summary: Overfit: train good, validation bad. Underfit: both bad. Use learning curves to tell them apart.
items.details: Overfitting fixes: more data, regularization (L1/L2, dropout), simpler model, early stopping, augmentation. Underfitting fixes: more features, more capacity, longer training, less regularization.
items.example: Training AUC 0.99, validation 0.78 → overfitting.

items.name: Catastrophic forgetting
items.summary: Fine-tuning on a narrow task erases general skills.
items.details: Mix in general examples (rehearsal), use PEFT so base weights stay frozen, lower the learning rate, and evaluate general tasks too.
items.example: Legal fine-tuning keeps general Q&A skills after adding 20% general data.

items.name: Combining models
items.summary: Bagging, boosting, stacking for accuracy; cascades and routing for cost.
items.details: Ensembles reduce variance or bias; cascades call an expensive model only when a cheap one is unsure.
items.example: A small model handles confident cases and escalates the rest.

items.name: Prompt engineering for customization
items.summary: Clear instructions, roles, few-shot examples, output schemas, chain-of-thought, and delimiters.
items.details: Inference parameters: temperature and top_p control randomness; maxTokens limits output; stop sequences end generation.
items.example: A JSON schema plus three examples makes extraction output parse reliably.
items.tip: Format problems → better prompt before fine-tuning.

items.name: Optimizing retrieval and embeddings
items.summary: Tune chunk size and overlap, number of results, hybrid search, reranking, and the embedding model.
items.details: Measure retrieval separately (context relevance, coverage, recall@k) before changing the generator.
items.example: Reranking the top 20 results puts the right passage in the top 3.

sections.group: Domain 2 · ML model and FM development
sections.title: Analyze and evaluate ML and AI systems
sections.summary: Task 2.3: experiments, baselines, shadow tests, explainability, convergence, metrics, LLM and RAG evaluation.

items.name: Classification metrics
items.summary: Precision (few false positives), recall (few false negatives), F1, accuracy, specificity, confusion matrix.
items.details: Pick the metric that matches the business cost of errors. Accuracy misleads on imbalanced data.
items.example: Cancer screening prioritizes recall; spam quarantine prioritizes precision.

items.name: ROC-AUC and PR-AUC
items.summary: Threshold-independent ranking quality; PR-AUC is more informative for rare positives.
items.details: Choose the operating threshold separately based on costs.
items.example: Two fraud models are compared by PR-AUC, then a threshold is set for 90% precision.

items.name: Regression metrics
items.summary: MAE (robust to outliers), RMSE (penalizes large errors), R², MAPE.
items.details: RMSE ≥ MAE; a big gap means some large errors.
items.example: Delivery times with storm outliers are judged by MAE.

items.name: Reproducible experiments
items.summary: Track code, data version, parameters, metrics, and prompts for every run.
items.details: MLflow on SageMaker AI, Bedrock evaluations, and Prompt Management versions make results repeatable.
items.example: Each prompt version links to its evaluation report.

items.name: Baselines and drift detection
items.summary: Compute statistics on training data; compare production data with PSI, KS, or divergence tests.
items.details: Data drift is a change in inputs; concept drift is a change in the input-to-label relationship and shows up as falling model quality.
items.example: PSI above 0.2 on a key feature triggers retraining.

items.name: Shadow variants vs A/B tests
items.summary: Shadow: copy of traffic, no user impact. A/B: real users split by weight to measure outcomes.
items.details: Use shadow to check latency and agreement safely, then A/B to measure business impact.
items.example: A new model runs in shadow, then gets 10% of real traffic.

items.name: Explaining model outputs
items.summary: SHAP for per-prediction attributions; partial dependence plots and global importance for overall effects.
items.details: SHAP values sum to the difference between a prediction and the baseline. Interpretable models (linear, shallow trees) can be explained directly.
items.example: A rejected applicant is told which three features lowered their score.

items.name: Debugging convergence
items.summary: NaN or exploding loss, vanishing gradients, plateaus, and oscillation.
items.details: Remedies: lower learning rate, gradient clipping, normalization layers, better initialization, ReLU-family activations, checking data for NaNs and label errors.
items.example: Huge gradient norms before NaN loss → clip gradients and lower the learning rate.

items.name: NLP metrics
items.summary: BLEU (translation, precision), ROUGE (summaries, recall), BERTScore (meaning), perplexity, cosine similarity.
items.details: N-gram metrics punish valid paraphrases; embedding-based metrics such as BERTScore reward matching meaning.
items.example: Correct but reworded summaries score low on ROUGE and high on BERTScore.

items.name: LLM evaluation
items.summary: Golden datasets, LLM-as-a-judge, human evaluation, and responsible AI metrics such as stereotyping.
items.details: Combine automated scoring at scale with human review of samples; track results over time.
items.example: A judge model scores 20,000 responses weekly; experts review 200.

items.name: Human-in-the-loop
items.summary: Route low-confidence or high-risk outputs to people; use human ratings for subjective quality.
items.details: Bedrock human evaluation jobs use your own team. (SageMaker A2I review loops are legacy for new customers.)
items.example: Loan decisions below 0.7 confidence are reviewed by an analyst.

items.name: Evaluating and monitoring RAG
items.summary: Retrieval: context relevance, coverage, recall@k. Generation: faithfulness, correctness, citation quality.
items.details: Evaluate retrieval separately to find the real cause of bad answers, and keep monitoring after launch.
items.example: Low context coverage shows the knowledge base is missing documents.

sections.group: Domain 3 · Deployment and orchestration of ML and AI workflows
sections.title: Manage deployment infrastructure
sections.summary: Task 3.1: compute targets, inference strategies, FM hosting, external models, agents, RAG configuration.

items.name: Choosing where to run inference
items.summary: Bedrock (serverless FMs), SageMaker AI endpoints (your models), Lambda (light logic), ECS/EKS (custom stacks).
items.details: Least operational overhead usually points to Bedrock for available FMs and SageMaker AI for custom models.
items.example: An available FM with unpredictable traffic → Bedrock on demand.

items.name: Real-time, serverless, async, or batch
items.summary: Latency need, traffic pattern, payload size, processing time, and idle cost decide.
items.details: Real-time: steady, low latency, GPUs. Serverless: intermittent, small, CPU. Async: up to 1 GB and 1 hour, queued. Batch: whole datasets on a schedule.
items.example: Nightly scoring of 40 million rows → batch transform.
items.tip: Memorize the four options’ limits.

items.name: Sharing endpoints
items.summary: Multi-model (many similar models), multi-container (mixed frameworks), pipelines (chains), inference components.
items.details: Sharing cuts cost for low-traffic models but adds noisy-neighbor and cold-load trade-offs.
items.example: 3,000 small customer models → multi-model endpoint.

items.name: FM deployment options
items.summary: Bedrock on demand, Provisioned Throughput, batch, Marketplace, Custom Model Import, or self-hosting on SageMaker AI.
items.details: Self-hosting gives control of the model, instance, and container at the cost of more operations.
items.example: A model fine-tuned elsewhere is imported into Bedrock to reuse the same APIs.

items.name: Models built outside AWS
items.summary: Upload artifacts to S3 and use prebuilt framework containers, or import supported FMs into Bedrock.
items.details: Package artifacts as model.tar.gz for SageMaker AI. Build a custom container only when no prebuilt one fits.
items.example: A laptop-trained scikit-learn model is hosted with the prebuilt scikit-learn container.

items.name: Deploying agents
items.summary: Host on AgentCore Runtime; connect tools through Gateway (MCP); talk to other agents with A2A.
items.details: Multi-agent patterns include a supervisor that delegates to specialist agents. Isolate sessions and give each agent only the tools it needs.
items.example: A planning agent delegates to specialist agents over A2A and calls tools over MCP.

items.name: FM hosting resources
items.summary: GPU memory ≈ parameters × bytes per parameter plus KV cache; shard with tensor parallelism; quantize to fit.
items.details: A 70B model in 16-bit needs about 140 GB for weights alone, so it spans several GPUs. Continuous batching raises throughput.
items.example: Tensor parallel degree 8 spreads a 70B model across 8 GPUs.

items.name: RAG retrieval configuration
items.summary: Number of results, search type, metadata filters, reranking, and query decomposition.
items.details: Retrieve more, then rerank to a few; filter by metadata; decompose multi-part questions.
items.example: A comparison question about two countries is decomposed into two sub-queries.

sections.group: Domain 3 · Deployment and orchestration of ML and AI workflows
sections.title: Provision and configure resources
sections.summary: Task 3.2: capacity models, IaC, containers, VPC endpoints, SDK deployment, scaling, knowledge bases, agents.

items.name: On-demand vs provisioned capacity
items.summary: Pay-per-use for spiky or low traffic; provisioned or committed capacity for steady high utilization.
items.details: Examples: Bedrock on demand vs Provisioned Throughput; serverless inference vs real-time instances; Savings Plans for steady SageMaker AI use.
items.example: A 10%-utilized Provisioned Throughput commitment isn’t renewed.

items.name: Automating provisioning
items.summary: CloudFormation or CDK stacks, with cross-stack outputs and parameters, deployed by pipelines.
items.details: Keep networking, security, and model stacks separate and connect them with exports or parameters.
items.example: Endpoint stacks import subnet IDs from the network stack.

items.name: Containers for ML
items.summary: Use AWS Deep Learning Containers when possible; custom images must follow the SageMaker contract.
items.details: Serving containers answer /ping and /invocations on port 8080 and load the model from /opt/ml/model. Keep images small and versioned in ECR.
items.example: A custom container fails health checks until /ping is implemented.

items.name: Endpoints inside a VPC
items.summary: Private subnets, security groups, an S3 gateway endpoint, and interface endpoints for SageMaker APIs.
items.details: No NAT or internet gateway is needed when VPC endpoints cover the services the workload calls.
items.example: An endpoint reads S3 and is invoked by in-VPC apps with no internet path.

items.name: Deploying programmatically
items.summary: SageMaker Python SDK (model.deploy), Boto3 (CreateModel → CreateEndpointConfig → CreateEndpoint), or the CLI.
items.details: Endpoint configurations are immutable; updates create a new configuration and call UpdateEndpoint.
items.example: A pipeline step deploys with Boto3 calls in the right order.

items.name: Choosing scaling metrics
items.summary: InvocationsPerInstance for short requests; concurrency for long or streaming ones; GPU metrics for GPU-bound models.
items.details: Test custom metrics before production and set cooldowns to avoid flapping.
items.example: An image generation endpoint scales on GPUUtilization.

items.name: Scaling GPU workloads
items.summary: Scale on GPU signals, use inference components (scale to zero), check quotas, and reserve capacity for training.
items.details: GPU capacity can be scarce; training plans or capacity reservations secure it for planned runs.
items.example: An endpoint’s rarely used model scales its copies to zero overnight.

items.name: Managing knowledge bases
items.summary: Vector store configuration, document indexing (sync), and retrieval tuning.
items.details: Track ingestion job results for failed documents; re-embed when changing the embedding model.
items.example: A sync report shows 12 PDFs failed to parse and need advanced parsing.

items.name: Building retrieval pipelines
items.summary: Retrieve, filter, rerank, and assemble the prompt yourself when you need control.
items.details: Add business rules and user context to the prompt; cite sources in the answer.
items.example: User profile data and retrieved passages are combined before calling the model.

items.name: Agent state management
items.summary: Short-term (session) and long-term (cross-session) memory, keyed by user and session.
items.details: AgentCore Memory provides both; custom state can live in DynamoDB. Don’t rely on the prompt alone for long histories.
items.example: A support agent recalls a customer’s past issues in a new session.

items.name: Agentic workflow infrastructure
items.summary: Runtime for hosting, Gateway for tools, Identity for auth, Memory for state, Observability for traces.
items.details: Add Policy to restrict tool use and Evaluations to score agent quality.
items.example: A customer service agent is assembled from five AgentCore services.

sections.group: Domain 3 · Deployment and orchestration of ML and AI workflows
sections.title: Automate orchestration and CI/CD
sections.summary: Task 3.3: deployment strategies, Code* services, jobs, testing, retraining, versioning of models, prompts, and agents.

items.name: Deployment strategies and rollback
items.summary: Blue/green (all at once, canary, linear), rolling, shadow, and A/B, with alarm-based rollback.
items.details: Canary tests a small share first; linear moves in equal steps; rolling avoids doubling capacity; shadow has no user impact.
items.example: A 20-GPU endpoint uses rolling updates because blue/green would exceed quotas.

items.name: CI/CD services
items.summary: CodePipeline orchestrates; CodeBuild builds and tests; CodeDeploy deploys; CodeConnections links GitHub.
items.details: Most permission failures in builds come from the CodeBuild or CodePipeline service role.
items.example: A GitHub merge starts a pipeline that builds, scans, and pushes an image.

items.name: Configuring training and inference jobs
items.summary: Image, instance type and count, input channels, output path, hyperparameters, volume KMS key, VPC, and limits.
items.details: Set max run time, spot settings, and checkpoint locations; use quotas that match the instance type.
items.example: A job sets a KMS key, private subnets, and spot with checkpoints.

items.name: Testing in ML pipelines
items.summary: Unit tests for code, data validation, model quality gates, integration and load tests before release.
items.details: Fail the pipeline automatically when a test or metric threshold fails.
items.example: A Condition step blocks registration when F1 < 0.85.

items.name: Retraining mechanisms
items.summary: Retrain on a schedule, on new data, or when drift or quality alarms fire.
items.details: EventBridge starts pipelines from schedules, S3 events, or CloudWatch alarm state changes. Gate deployment on evaluation results.
items.example: A drift alarm starts retraining, and approval starts deployment.

items.name: Model versioning for repeatability and audits
items.summary: Model Registry groups and versions; MLflow registry; lineage from data to endpoint.
items.details: Record data version, code version, metrics, approver, and deployment history.
items.example: Auditors trace a deployed model back to its training data and approval.

items.name: Managing prompts
items.summary: Version prompts, test variants, and pin production to a version.
items.details: Treat prompts like code: review, test, version, and roll back.
items.example: A prompt change is rolled back by pointing the app to the previous version ARN.

items.name: Agent deployment and versions
items.summary: Pipelines build and deploy agent code; AgentCore versions are immutable and endpoints pin them.
items.details: Promote by updating the production endpoint after tests pass; roll back by pointing it at the earlier version.
items.example: PROD moves from version 3 to 4 only after evaluation passes.

items.name: AI testing and prompt testing
items.summary: Golden datasets, regression evaluations, adversarial (red-team) prompts, and safety checks in CI.
items.details: Automated evaluation with a pass/fail threshold catches regressions before promotion.
items.example: 300 golden questions run on every prompt change.

items.name: Automating fine-tuned model releases
items.summary: Each customization job produces a new model ARN; register, evaluate, and deploy it through the pipeline.
items.details: Keep the previous custom model deployed until the new one passes evaluation.
items.example: A monthly fine-tuning run is promoted only if it beats the current model.

items.name: Orchestrating RAG refreshes
items.summary: Sequence ETL, knowledge base sync, validation, and alerts with Step Functions or EventBridge.
items.details: Sync only after upstream data is complete; alert on failed ingestion.
items.example: A Step Functions workflow runs ETL, starts the sync, and alerts on failure.

items.name: Choosing an orchestrator
items.summary: SageMaker Pipelines (ML-native, lineage), Step Functions (any AWS service), MWAA (existing Airflow).
items.details: Pick the tool the team already runs when the question stresses minimal change.
items.example: Hundreds of existing Airflow DAGs → MWAA.

sections.group: Domain 4 · Operating, monitoring, and securing ML and AI solutions
sections.title: Monitor model inference and performance
sections.summary: Task 4.1: what to monitor, drift types, workflow failures, A/B tests, agents, and FM quality.

items.name: What to monitor
items.summary: Infrastructure (latency, errors, utilization), data (drift), model (quality), business KPIs, and cost.
items.details: Each layer needs its own signal and alarm; a healthy endpoint can still serve a degraded model.
items.example: Latency is fine but precision has dropped for two weeks.

items.name: Types of drift
items.summary: Data (covariate) drift, concept drift, label (prior) drift, and feature attribution drift.
items.details: Detect data drift with statistical tests against a baseline; detect concept drift through model quality once labels arrive.
items.example: Feature importance shifting to postcode signals attribution drift.

items.name: Monitoring workflows and data processing
items.summary: Alert on failed pipeline executions, jobs, and unusual data volumes.
items.details: EventBridge rules catch status changes; CloudWatch anomaly detection catches unusual record counts.
items.example: An email arrives minutes after a nightly pipeline fails.

items.name: Monitoring A/B tests
items.summary: Compare per-variant metrics and business outcomes before shifting more traffic.
items.details: Make sure the sample is large enough and the test runs long enough to be meaningful.
items.example: A 10% variant runs for two weeks before promotion.

items.name: Monitoring agents
items.summary: Tool failures, loops, coordination failures, truncated streaming, latency per step, and tokens per session.
items.details: Agent traces show each step; alarms on tool error rates and stopReason max_tokens catch silent failures.
items.example: Traces show the agent retried a failing tool five times.

items.name: Monitoring FM quality
items.summary: Scheduled evaluations on sampled traffic, user feedback, guardrail intervention rates, and token metrics.
items.details: Quality can drift as user questions change even when the model doesn’t.
items.example: A weekly judge-model evaluation shows correctness falling on new product questions.

sections.group: Domain 4 · Operating, monitoring, and securing ML and AI solutions
sections.title: Optimize infrastructure cost and performance
sections.summary: Task 4.2: instance choice, troubleshooting tools, dashboards, capacity, cost tools, purchasing, FM and agent costs.

items.name: Choosing inference instances
items.summary: CPU for trees and small models; GPU for large deep models; Inferentia for cheaper compiled inference.
items.details: Right-size from utilization; idle GPUs are the most common waste.
items.example: An XGBoost endpoint moves from ml.g5 to ml.c7g.

items.name: Troubleshooting tools
items.summary: CloudWatch metrics and logs, X-Ray traces, AgentCore Observability, and Inference Recommender.
items.details: Separate model time from overhead (ModelLatency vs OverheadLatency) and trace each hop.
items.example: X-Ray shows most latency in the retrieval step.

items.name: Dashboards
items.summary: CloudWatch dashboards for operations; Quick Sight for business stakeholders.
items.details: Put the key metrics and their alarms on one screen per service.
items.example: One dashboard shows latency, errors, tokens, and pipeline status.

items.name: Capacity for cost, performance, and reliability
items.summary: Auto scaling, multiple instances across AZs, quotas, throttling handling, and cross-Region inference.
items.details: Two or more instances for availability; retries with backoff for throttles; raise quotas ahead of launches.
items.example: An endpoint gains a second instance in another AZ.

items.name: Cost management tools
items.summary: Budgets (alerts and actions), Cost Explorer, cost allocation tags, and Cost Anomaly Detection.
items.details: Tag everything by team and project; alert on forecasts, not just actuals.
items.example: A budget action stops new SageMaker resources at 100% of spend.

items.name: Purchasing options
items.summary: On-Demand, SageMaker AI Savings Plans, managed spot training, Bedrock Provisioned Throughput and reserved tiers.
items.details: Commit only to steady baseline usage; keep spiky usage on demand.
items.example: A 1-year SageMaker AI Savings Plan covers the always-on baseline.

items.name: FM inference cost drivers
items.summary: Input and output tokens, model size, context length, request volume, and service tier.
items.details: Output tokens usually cost more than input tokens; long system prompts are paid on every call unless cached.
items.example: Halving the system prompt cuts monthly Bedrock cost by a third.

items.name: Reducing FM costs
items.summary: Prompt caching, intelligent routing, batch inference, Flex tier, smaller or distilled models, shorter outputs.
items.details: Measure quality after each change so savings don’t hide regressions.
items.example: Batch inference handles an archive job at a lower price.

items.name: Agent resource consumption
items.summary: Tokens and tool calls per session, loop detection, and runtime CPU and memory.
items.details: Cap iterations, trim context, and alert on sessions with unusual token use.
items.example: An agent stuck in a tool loop is caught by a tokens-per-session alarm.

items.name: AI-specific cost patterns
items.summary: Token usage, embedding computation, and vector storage size and tier.
items.details: Avoid re-embedding unchanged content, reduce dimensions when recall allows, and move cold vectors to S3 Vectors.
items.example: Incremental syncs replace a nightly full re-embed of 2 million documents.

sections.group: Domain 4 · Operating, monitoring, and securing ML and AI solutions
sections.title: Secure ML and AI workloads
sections.summary: Task 4.3: secure CI/CD, least privilege, IAM, auditing, troubleshooting, isolation, AI risks, credentials, safeguards.

items.name: Securing CI/CD
items.summary: Scan images and code (Inspector), use least-privilege pipeline roles, and keep secrets out of builds.
items.details: Block deployment on critical findings; keep build artifacts in versioned, encrypted storage.
items.example: A pipeline stops when Inspector finds a critical CVE in the image.

items.name: Least privilege to ML artifacts
items.summary: Scope access to specific S3 prefixes, KMS keys, model packages, and endpoints.
items.details: Separate roles for data access, training, approval, and deployment.
items.example: The fraud training role can’t read the marketing data prefix.

items.name: IAM policies and roles
items.summary: Execution roles for jobs and endpoints; task roles for apps; condition keys to enforce settings.
items.details: Use roles (temporary credentials) instead of long-term access keys wherever possible.
items.example: An ECS task role lets an app call Bedrock without stored keys.

items.name: Monitoring, auditing, and compliance
items.summary: CloudTrail for API activity, Config for configuration compliance, invocation logging for prompts and responses.
items.details: Keep logs in protected, encrypted buckets with retention that matches regulations.
items.example: Config flags an endpoint without encryption; CloudTrail shows who created it.

items.name: Troubleshooting security issues
items.summary: AccessDenied usually means a missing permission, a key policy, an SCP, a VPC endpoint policy, or a trust policy.
items.details: Check each layer: identity policy, resource policy, KMS key policy, SCPs, permission boundaries, and endpoint policies.
items.example: A job reading SSE-KMS data needs kms:Decrypt as well as s3:GetObject.

items.name: Network isolation
items.summary: Private subnets, security groups, VPC endpoints, and the network isolation setting for containers.
items.details: Encrypt traffic between distributed training nodes with inter-container traffic encryption.
items.example: Third-party training code runs with network isolation.

items.name: AI-specific security risks
items.summary: Prompt injection, data poisoning, sensitive data leakage, model extraction or inversion, and insecure output handling.
items.details: Mitigate with guardrails, input validation, least-privilege tools, output validation, and access controls on training data.
items.example: An agent’s SQL tool uses parameterized queries so injected text can’t run commands.

items.name: Credentials for FMs
items.summary: IAM roles for production; short-term Bedrock API keys for exploration; long-term keys only with expiry and rotation.
items.details: Restrict API key types with IAM conditions where needed.
items.example: Developers test with short-term keys; services use roles.

items.name: Safeguards and responsible AI
items.summary: Guardrails (content, topics, PII, grounding, automated reasoning) plus human review for high-risk outputs.
items.details: Apply guardrails to both inputs and outputs; log interventions to tune them.
items.example: PII in answers is masked and ungrounded answers are blocked.

sections.title: MLA-C02 beta format & scoring
sections.summary: What to expect on exam day for the beta (exam code ME1-C02).

items.name: 85 questions in 170 minutes (beta)
items.summary: The beta costs $75, is in English only, and is delivered by Pearson VUE at a test center or online.
items.details: Beta exams include extra items that AWS evaluates; they don’t affect your score and you can’t tell which they are. Two minutes per question is the average pace.
items.example: Finish a first pass by about 120 minutes, leaving 50 minutes for flagged questions.
items.tip: Don’t sink more than 3–4 minutes into any single question on the first pass.

items.name: General availability format
items.summary: The guide describes 50 scored plus 15 unscored questions, a scaled score of 100–1,000, and 720 to pass.
items.details: Scoring is compensatory: strong domains can offset weaker ones. Beta results take longer than usual because AWS sets the passing standard after the beta closes.
items.example: Weight your study 28 / 24 / 24 / 24 across the four domains.

items.name: Two question types
items.summary: Multiple choice (1 of 4) and multiple response (2 or more of 5 or more). No ordering, matching, or case studies.
items.details: MLA-C01 had ordering, matching, and case-study questions; the MLA-C02 guide lists only multiple choice and multiple response. There is no partial credit.
items.example: “Which TWO actions…? (Select TWO.)” needs both correct answers.

items.name: Key dates
items.summary: Beta from September 29, 2026; MLA-C01 in English ended September 28, 2026; GA planned for January 14, 2027.
items.details: MLA-C01 stays available in Japanese, Korean, and Simplified Chinese until general availability.
items.example: If you pass the beta, the certification is the same MLA credential, valid for 3 years.

items.name: What’s new versus MLA-C01
items.summary: Same four domains; about 45 new skills on generative AI, RAG, agents, FM evaluation, and FM costs and security.
items.details: Removed: SageMaker Neo and edge optimization, bring-your-own-container, model-size reduction, and EventBridge infrastructure monitoring. Expect Bedrock, knowledge bases, AgentCore, Guardrails, and evaluations alongside classic SageMaker AI topics.
items.example: Study RAG and agents as seriously as training and deployment.

sections.title: Services that changed recently
sections.summary: Features closed to new customers in 2025–2026 and how to answer questions about them.

items.name: SageMaker AI features closed to new customers (July 30, 2026)
items.summary: Model Monitor, Clarify, Debugger, Ground Truth, A2I, Role Manager, and Studio Lab.
items.details: Existing customers keep using them. The MLA-C02 guide no longer names them; it describes the skills instead (drift detection pipelines, explaining outputs, debugging convergence, labeling). AWS’s replacements: MLflow, SHAP and standard bias formulas, TensorBoard, CloudWatch, and Bedrock Evaluations.
items.example: A scenario that says the team “already uses Model Monitor” can still have it as the answer.
items.tip: Learn the concepts behind these features; they are still tested.

items.name: Bedrock Agents Classic (July 30, 2026)
items.summary: New accounts can’t create Classic agents; AWS recommends Bedrock AgentCore.
items.details: Existing agents keep working in maintenance mode with no planned end date.
items.example: Agent hosting, tools, and memory in new scenarios → AgentCore.

items.name: CodeGuru Reviewer and CodeGuru Security (November 2025)
items.summary: Reviewer closed to new customers; Security was discontinued. The guide still mentions CodeGuru.
items.details: AWS points to Amazon Inspector for code and dependency scanning and Amazon Q Developer for code review. CodeGuru Profiler remains.
items.example: Scan images and code in CI/CD → Inspector.

items.name: Other changes worth knowing
items.summary: CodeCommit is fully available again; DevOps Guru is being retired (support ends September 30, 2027).
items.details: The vault-based Amazon Glacier service closed to new customers (S3 Glacier storage classes are unaffected). Comprehend topic modeling and event detection, and Rekognition streaming events, closed to new customers in April 2026.
items.example: Prefer current services when two answers otherwise look equally valid.

sections.title: Qualifier keywords
sections.summary: Words in the question that decide between otherwise valid answers.

items.name: LEAST operational overhead / LEAST effort
items.summary: Pick the most managed option: Bedrock over self-hosting, serverless over instances, built-in over custom.
items.details: Options that mention building containers, managing clusters, or writing custom code are usually wrong for this qualifier.
items.example: Track experiments → managed MLflow, not a self-hosted tracking server on EC2.

items.name: MOST cost-effective
items.summary: The cheapest option that still meets every stated requirement.
items.details: Match the pricing model to the traffic: serverless or on demand for spiky use, batch for offline work, Savings Plans or provisioned capacity for steady use, spot for interruptible training.
items.example: A model idle most of the day → serverless inference, not an always-on endpoint.

items.name: Lowest latency / real time
items.summary: Real-time endpoints, smaller models, streaming responses, caching, and keeping data close.
items.details: Near-real-time (seconds to minutes) allows Firehose or async patterns; real-time (milliseconds) needs synchronous endpoints and online stores.
items.example: Sub-second fraud scoring reads features from the online store.

items.name: MOST secure / compliance
items.summary: Least privilege, encryption with customer managed keys, private networking, and auditing.
items.details: Prefer roles over long-term keys, VPC endpoints over internet paths, and preventive controls over detective ones.
items.example: Production apps call Bedrock with IAM roles, not long-term API keys.

items.name: Scalable / minimal code changes
items.summary: Choose services that scale automatically or reuse what the team already runs.
items.details: “Existing Airflow DAGs” → MWAA; “existing Spark code” → EMR; “existing PyTorch script” → script mode.
items.example: A team with a working PyTorch script trains on SageMaker AI with script mode instead of rewriting the model.

sections.title: Answering technique
sections.summary: How to work through long scenario questions quickly.

items.name: Read the last sentence first
items.summary: Find what is being asked and the qualifier, then read the scenario for constraints.
items.details: Underline constraints mentally: payload size, latency, traffic pattern, data residency, existing tools, and team skills.
items.example: “…with the LEAST operational overhead?” tells you to favor managed services before you read the details.

items.name: Eliminate, then compare two
items.summary: Remove options that break any requirement; compare the remaining two against the qualifier.
items.details: Watch for options that are true statements but don’t solve the stated problem.
items.example: Both remaining options reduce cost, but only one keeps the 100 ms latency target.

items.name: Multiple response questions
items.summary: Judge each option on its own; the correct ones usually address different parts of the problem.
items.details: If two options say the same thing in different words, they are rarely both correct.
items.example: Fix overfitting → early stopping AND regularization.

items.name: Flag and move on
items.summary: Answer every question, flag uncertain ones, and come back with fresh eyes.
items.details: Blank answers score zero; a reasoned guess has a chance.
items.example: With 10 minutes left, pick an answer for every flagged question before reviewing any of them.

sections.title: Data triggers
sections.summary: Phrases that point to a specific data service or technique.

items.name: “Streaming JSON to S3 as Parquet, no code”
items.summary: Amazon Data Firehose with record format conversion.
items.details: Firehose buffers records, converts them with a Glue table schema, and delivers files with no servers.
items.example: Clickstream JSON lands in S3 as Parquet every five minutes.

items.name: “Rolling window per key on a stream”
items.summary: Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink.
items.details: Flink keeps state per key and computes windowed aggregations continuously.
items.example: Trips per driver in the last 15 minutes update the online feature store.

items.name: “One shard throttled, others idle”
items.summary: Use a high-cardinality partition key.
items.details: A skewed key sends most records to one shard; adding shards alone doesn’t help.
items.example: Device ID replaces device model as the partition key.

items.name: “Training waits a long time downloading data”
items.summary: FastFile (or Pipe) input mode.
items.details: File mode copies the whole dataset before training; streaming modes start immediately.
items.example: A 35-minute download disappears after switching to FastFile.

items.name: “GPUs starved reading terabytes every epoch”
items.summary: FSx for Lustre linked to the S3 bucket.
items.details: Parallel, high-throughput reads keep GPUs busy across many epochs.
items.example: A 40 TB image dataset is read at full speed every epoch.

items.name: “Which buckets contain PII?”
items.summary: Amazon Macie.
items.details: Macie scans S3 objects and reports where sensitive data is stored.
items.example: Macie finds customer phone numbers in 2 of 40 buckets.

items.name: “Stop bad data before retraining”
items.summary: AWS Glue Data Quality rules in the ETL job.
items.details: Rules such as Completeness can fail the job before data reaches training.
items.example: A file with 40% nulls in a key column stops the pipeline.

items.name: “Hide some columns from some analysts”
items.summary: AWS Lake Formation fine-grained permissions.
items.details: Column-, row-, and cell-level grants are enforced by Athena and other engines.
items.example: Fraud analysts can’t see date of birth or address.

items.name: “Hundreds of millions of vectors, rarely queried, lowest cost”
items.summary: Amazon S3 Vectors.
items.details: Serverless vector buckets with sub-second queries at a fraction of cluster cost.
items.example: A legal archive becomes searchable without an OpenSearch cluster.

sections.title: Modeling triggers
sections.summary: Phrases that point to an algorithm, customization method, or evaluation tool.

items.name: “Facts change daily” or “must cite sources”
items.summary: RAG with a knowledge base.
items.details: Retrieval uses current documents at query time and returns citations; fine-tuning can’t keep up.
items.example: Product prices that change several times a day are answered from synced documents.

items.name: “Consistent tone, structure, or format”
items.summary: Fine-tuning on labeled examples.
items.details: Fine-tuning changes behavior; try a better prompt first when least effort matters.
items.example: 8,000 approved letters teach a consistent customer letter format.

items.name: “Smaller, cheaper model with similar quality, no labels”
items.summary: Distillation.
items.details: A teacher model generates responses to your prompts to train a smaller student.
items.example: Logged chatbot prompts distill a large model into a cheaper one.

items.name: “Lots of unlabeled domain text”
items.summary: Continued pre-training.
items.details: Unlabeled documents adapt a model to a domain’s vocabulary without labels.
items.example: Millions of research reports teach internal terminology.

items.name: “Thousands of related time series”
items.summary: DeepAR.
items.details: DeepAR learns one model across related series, which helps series with short histories.
items.example: Daily demand forecasts for 20,000 products.

items.name: “Unsupervised anomaly scores”
items.summary: Random Cut Forest.
items.details: RCF assigns each record an anomaly score without labels.
items.example: Logging-error spikes in server metrics are found and removed.

items.name: “Many expensive trials; stop weak ones early”
items.summary: Hyperband tuning.
items.details: Hyperband reallocates resources from weak to promising configurations.
items.example: A 3-hour-per-trial search fits within the budget.

items.name: “Track and compare experiments”
items.summary: Managed MLflow on SageMaker AI.
items.details: MLflow logs parameters, metrics, and artifacts and registers the best model.
items.example: Hundreds of runs are compared in one UI.

items.name: “Score thousands of responses for helpfulness”
items.summary: LLM-as-a-judge evaluation.
items.details: An evaluator model scores and explains each response at scale.
items.example: 20,000 weekly chatbot answers are scored without human reviewers.

items.name: “Correct paraphrases score badly on ROUGE”
items.summary: BERTScore.
items.details: Embedding-based similarity rewards matching meaning instead of matching words.
items.example: Reworded but correct summaries score well.

sections.title: Deployment and operations triggers
sections.summary: Phrases that point to an inference option, release strategy, or monitoring tool.

items.name: “Payloads up to 1 GB” or “20 minutes per request”
items.summary: Asynchronous inference.
items.details: Async queues requests, handles large inputs and long processing, and can scale to zero.
items.example: 800 MB videos are analyzed and the app is notified by SNS.

items.name: “Infrequent traffic, cold starts acceptable”
items.summary: Serverless Inference.
items.details: Scales to zero and bills per use; no GPUs.
items.example: A few hundred requests a day cost almost nothing.

items.name: “Score the whole dataset nightly”
items.summary: Batch transform.
items.details: No persistent endpoint; compute stops when the job ends.
items.example: 40 million accounts are scored overnight.

items.name: “Thousands of small models”
items.summary: Multi-model endpoint.
items.details: Same-framework models share instances and load from S3 on demand.
items.example: 3,000 per-customer models share one endpoint.

items.name: “Compare on live traffic with no customer impact”
items.summary: Shadow test.
items.details: The shadow variant receives copies of requests but its responses aren’t returned.
items.example: A new fraud model runs in shadow for a week.

items.name: “Gradual update without doubling capacity”
items.summary: Rolling deployment.
items.details: Rolling updates replace instances in batches with alarm-based rollback.
items.example: A 20-GPU fleet updates in 25% batches.

items.name: “Deploy automatically when a model is approved”
items.summary: EventBridge rule on the model package state change.
items.details: Model Registry emits events when approval status changes.
items.example: Approval starts CodePipeline within seconds.

items.name: “Host an agent with isolated sessions”
items.summary: AgentCore Runtime.
items.details: Serverless hosting for any framework with a microVM per session.
items.example: A Strands agent serves thousands of users safely.

items.name: “Expose existing APIs as MCP tools”
items.summary: AgentCore Gateway.
items.details: Gateway converts OpenAPI, Smithy, and Lambda targets into MCP tools with auth.
items.example: 40 internal APIs become agent tools.

items.name: “Keep every prompt and response”
items.summary: Bedrock model invocation logging.
items.details: CloudTrail doesn’t record prompt and response content; invocation logging does.
items.example: Audit logs of all prompts are stored in S3.

items.name: “Answers not supported by retrieved sources”
items.summary: Contextual grounding check in Guardrails.
items.details: Grounding and relevance thresholds block or flag unsupported answers.
items.example: An invented refund period is blocked.

items.name: “Same long prompt prefix on every call”
items.summary: Prompt caching.
items.details: Cached prefixes cost less and process faster on later calls.
items.example: A 30,000-token manual is cached for every question.

sections.title: SageMaker AI inference options
sections.summary: Real-time vs serverless vs asynchronous vs batch transform.

items.name: Real-time endpoints
items.summary: Persistent instances, lowest latency, GPUs, steady traffic.
items.details: You pay for instances while they run, even when idle.
items.example: An interactive assistant on a GPU endpoint.

items.name: Serverless Inference
items.summary: Scales to zero, 1–6 GB memory, no GPUs, possible cold starts.
items.details: Good for intermittent CPU traffic; provisioned concurrency reduces cold starts.
items.example: A rarely used scoring API.

items.name: Asynchronous inference
items.summary: Queued requests, payloads to 1 GB, up to 1 hour, can scale to zero.
items.details: Input and output go through S3; SNS can notify on completion.
items.example: Video or long document analysis.

items.name: Batch transform
items.summary: Whole datasets from S3, no persistent endpoint.
items.details: Best for scheduled offline scoring.
items.example: Nightly churn scores for every account.

sections.title: Bedrock inference choices
sections.summary: On-demand tiers vs cross-Region inference vs Provisioned Throughput vs batch.

items.name: On demand (Standard, Priority, Flex)
items.summary: Pay per token; Priority is faster at a premium; Flex is cheaper but slower.
items.details: Standard is the default; choose a tier per request.
items.example: Live chat on Standard, overnight tagging on Flex.

items.name: Cross-Region inference
items.summary: Routes requests across Regions for throughput: geographic for residency, global for savings.
items.details: No extra routing cost; CloudTrail shows where each request ran.
items.example: An EU app absorbs peaks with the EU profile.

items.name: Provisioned Throughput
items.summary: Dedicated model units with optional 1- or 6-month commitments.
items.details: Worth it only at steady, high utilization.
items.example: A 24/7 high-volume workload with throttling.

items.name: Batch inference
items.summary: Asynchronous jobs from S3 at a discount.
items.details: Results arrive in hours, not seconds.
items.example: Summarizing 2 million archived documents.

sections.title: Data preparation tools
sections.summary: Glue vs DataBrew vs Data Wrangler vs EMR vs Athena.

items.name: AWS Glue
items.summary: Serverless Spark ETL and the Data Catalog.
items.details: Production ETL with schedules, bookmarks, and data quality rules.
items.example: Nightly joins of RDS and S3 data.

items.name: AWS Glue DataBrew
items.summary: No-code cleaning with recipes and profiles.
items.details: For analysts who don’t write code.
items.example: Weekly cleaning of a sales file.

items.name: Data Wrangler (in Canvas)
items.summary: ML-focused visual preparation with quality reports and export to pipelines.
items.details: For data scientists building features interactively.
items.example: A flow exported to SageMaker Pipelines.

items.name: Amazon EMR
items.summary: Big Spark or Hadoop clusters with full control.
items.details: For existing Spark code and custom libraries at huge scale.
items.example: Hundreds of PySpark jobs with custom JARs.

items.name: Amazon Athena
items.summary: Serverless SQL on S3.
items.details: For exploration and CTAS extracts, priced per data scanned.
items.example: A CTAS query builds a Parquet training set.

sections.title: Streaming services
sections.summary: Kinesis Data Streams vs Data Firehose vs Managed Service for Apache Flink.

items.name: Kinesis Data Streams
items.summary: Durable streams for custom consumers within milliseconds.
items.details: You write or choose the consumers (Lambda, Flink, apps).
items.example: A Lambda consumer updates fraud features.

items.name: Data Firehose
items.summary: Managed delivery to S3, Redshift, or OpenSearch with buffering and conversion.
items.details: Near-real-time (seconds to minutes), no code.
items.example: Clickstream to Parquet in S3.

items.name: Managed Service for Apache Flink
items.summary: Stateful, windowed processing and stream joins.
items.details: For continuous aggregations with state.
items.example: Per-driver trip counts over 15 minutes.

sections.title: Vector stores
sections.summary: OpenSearch vs pgvector vs S3 Vectors vs Neptune Analytics.

items.name: OpenSearch Service
items.summary: Low latency, high query volume, hybrid search, rich filters.
items.details: Managed domains or Serverless collections.
items.example: A support assistant with exact error-code matching.

items.name: pgvector (Aurora or RDS PostgreSQL)
items.summary: Vectors beside relational data with SQL joins.
items.details: No new database for teams already on PostgreSQL.
items.example: Semantic search on product rows.

items.name: S3 Vectors
items.summary: Lowest cost for huge, infrequently queried sets with sub-second queries.
items.details: Serverless; integrates with Bedrock knowledge bases.
items.example: A 400-million-chunk legal archive.

items.name: Neptune Analytics
items.summary: Graph plus vectors for GraphRAG.
items.details: For multi-hop relationship questions.
items.example: Drug–trial–compound questions.

sections.title: Orchestrators
sections.summary: SageMaker Pipelines vs Step Functions vs MWAA vs EventBridge.

items.name: SageMaker Pipelines
items.summary: ML-native steps, caching, lineage, and Model Registry integration.
items.details: Best for training workflows built around SageMaker AI.
items.example: Process, train, evaluate, and register weekly.

items.name: Step Functions
items.summary: General workflows across 200+ services with retries and branching.
items.details: Best when a workflow spans many services.
items.example: ETL, then knowledge base sync, then alerts.

items.name: Amazon MWAA
items.summary: Managed Apache Airflow for existing DAGs.
items.details: Best when the team already runs Airflow.
items.example: ML tasks added to existing data DAGs.

items.name: EventBridge
items.summary: Schedules and event rules that start workflows; not a workflow engine.
items.details: Triggers pipelines from schedules, approvals, or alarms.
items.example: A drift alarm starts retraining.

sections.title: Logging and auditing
sections.summary: CloudTrail vs Bedrock invocation logging vs CloudWatch vs Config.

items.name: CloudTrail
items.summary: Who called which API, when, and from where.
items.details: Records management events by default; data events are opt-in.
items.example: Who updated the endpoint last Tuesday.

items.name: Bedrock invocation logging
items.summary: Prompt and response content plus token counts.
items.details: Off by default; logs to CloudWatch Logs or S3.
items.example: Every prompt kept for audits.

items.name: CloudWatch
items.summary: Metrics, logs, alarms, and dashboards.
items.details: Operational health and alerting.
items.example: Latency alarm on an endpoint.

items.name: AWS Config
items.summary: Resource configuration history and compliance rules.
items.details: Detects noncompliant settings continuously.
items.example: Endpoint configurations without KMS are flagged.

sections.title: Sensitive data tools
sections.summary: Macie vs Comprehend PII vs Glue Detect PII vs Guardrails sensitive information filters.

items.name: Macie
items.summary: Finds where sensitive data is stored in S3.
items.details: Discovery and reporting, not redaction.
items.example: An inventory of buckets holding PII.

items.name: Comprehend PII
items.summary: Detects and redacts PII in free text.
items.details: Real-time calls or batch redaction jobs.
items.example: Transcripts redacted before fine-tuning.

items.name: Glue Detect PII
