items.summary: Masks or hashes sensitive columns during ETL.
items.details: Tabular pipelines.
items.example: Emails hashed in a training table.

items.name: Guardrails sensitive information filters
items.summary: Blocks or masks PII in model inputs and outputs at run time.
items.details: Protects live generative AI traffic.
items.example: Phone numbers masked in assistant answers.

sections.title: Security services
sections.summary: Inspector vs GuardDuty vs Secrets Manager vs Parameter Store.

items.name: Amazon Inspector
items.summary: Vulnerabilities in container images, Lambda code and packages, and EC2.
items.details: Use in CI/CD to block critical findings.
items.example: A critical CVE blocks an inference image.

items.name: Amazon GuardDuty
items.summary: Threat detection from account, network, and data activity.
items.details: Not in the MLA-C02 scope; don’t pick it for vulnerability scanning.
items.example: Unusual API calls from a strange IP address.

items.name: Secrets Manager
items.summary: Secrets with automatic rotation.
items.details: Read at run time with an IAM role.
items.example: A partner API key used by a processing job.

items.name: Parameter Store
items.summary: Configuration values and simple secrets without built-in rotation.
items.details: Cheaper and simpler for settings.
items.example: An approved instance type read by a pipeline.

sections.title: AgentCore components
sections.summary: Which component does what.

items.name: Runtime
items.summary: Hosts agents and MCP servers with session isolation.
items.details: Serverless, framework-agnostic, long sessions.
items.example: A Strands agent in production.

items.name: Gateway
items.summary: APIs and Lambda functions as MCP tools, with auth and tool search.
items.details: One entry point for tools, agents, and model routing.
items.example: 40 APIs exposed as tools.

items.name: Memory
items.summary: Short-term session context and long-term preferences.
items.details: Managed extraction strategies for long-term memory.
items.example: Seat preferences remembered next month.

items.name: Identity
items.summary: Inbound user auth and outbound OAuth or API keys for tools.
items.details: Per-user tokens never sit in agent code.
items.example: Tickets created on behalf of each user.

items.name: Observability
items.summary: Traces of steps, tool calls, latency, and errors.
items.details: Visible in CloudWatch generative AI observability.
items.example: A failing tool found in traces.

items.name: Policy and Evaluations
items.summary: Control which tools agents may call; score agent quality.
items.details: Policies sit outside the agent code.
items.example: Refunds above a limit are blocked.

sections.title: API Gateway vs AgentCore Gateway
sections.summary: Two different “gateways”.

items.name: Amazon API Gateway
items.summary: Front door for REST, HTTP, and WebSocket APIs used by apps and partners.
items.details: Auth, throttling, usage plans, and caching for API clients.
items.example: Partners call a scoring API with keys.

items.name: AgentCore Gateway
items.summary: Turns APIs and Lambda functions into MCP tools that agents discover and call.
items.details: Built for agent tool use, with inbound and outbound auth.
items.example: An agent calls internal APIs as tools.

sections.title: Accelerators
sections.summary: GPU vs Inferentia vs Trainium vs CPU.

items.name: GPU instances (G and P families)
items.summary: General deep learning training and inference with the widest framework support.
items.details: P for large training; G for inference and lighter training.
items.example: An 8B LLM served on ml.g5.

items.name: Inferentia (Inf2)
items.summary: Lower-cost inference for Neuron-compiled models.
items.details: Compile with the Neuron SDK first.
items.example: A transformer served more cheaply on Inf2.

items.name: Trainium (Trn1, Trn2)
items.summary: Lower-cost training for Neuron-compiled models.
items.details: For long, large training runs.
items.example: Weeks-long LLM training at lower cost.

items.name: CPU instances (C, M, R families)
items.summary: Tree models, small models, and preprocessing.
items.details: Usually the cheapest choice when GPUs sit idle.
items.example: XGBoost moved from ml.g5 to ml.c7g.

sections.title: Customization methods
sections.summary: Prompting vs RAG vs fine-tuning vs continued pre-training vs distillation vs RFT.

items.name: Prompt engineering
items.summary: Instructions and examples; cheapest and fastest.
items.details: Try it first for format and behavior problems.
items.example: A JSON schema plus three examples.

items.name: RAG
items.summary: Adds current, citable knowledge at query time.
items.details: No model training; keep the knowledge base synced.
items.example: Answers about today’s prices.

items.name: Fine-tuning
items.summary: Labeled pairs change behavior, style, and format.
items.details: Needs good labeled data and evaluation.
items.example: Consistent customer letters.

items.name: Continued pre-training
items.summary: Unlabeled text adapts a model to a domain.
items.details: Needs a large corpus; offered for a limited set of models.
items.example: Internal research vocabulary.

items.name: Distillation
items.summary: A teacher model trains a smaller student from your prompts.
items.details: Cuts cost and latency while keeping quality on your use case.
items.example: A cheaper ticket classifier.

items.name: Reinforcement fine-tuning
items.summary: Reward functions score responses instead of labels.
items.details: Useful when correctness can be checked automatically.
items.example: Generated SQL rewarded when it runs correctly.

sections.title: Distributed training
sections.summary: Data parallel vs model parallel vs sharded data parallel.

items.name: Data parallel
items.summary: Each GPU holds the full model and a slice of the data.
items.details: Use when the model fits on one GPU and the data is huge.
items.example: 50 million images train in a day instead of six.

items.name: Model or tensor parallel
items.summary: The model itself is split across GPUs.
items.details: Use when the model doesn’t fit on one GPU.
items.example: A 70B model split across 8 GPUs.

items.name: Sharded data parallel (FSDP)
items.summary: Parameters, gradients, and optimizer states are sharded across GPUs.
items.details: Large models with data-parallel style training.
items.example: Fine-tuning a 70B model without OOM errors.

sections.title: Drift and monitoring types
sections.summary: Data drift vs concept drift vs bias drift vs feature attribution drift.

items.name: Data (covariate) drift
items.summary: Input distributions change.
items.details: Compare with a training baseline using PSI or KS tests.
items.example: Average basket size doubles after a promotion.

items.name: Concept drift
items.summary: The relationship between inputs and labels changes.
items.details: Shows up as falling model quality once labels arrive.
items.example: Fraudsters change tactics, so old patterns stop working.

items.name: Bias drift
items.summary: Fairness metrics between groups change over time.
items.details: Track per-group outcomes and error rates.
items.example: Approval rates diverge between age groups.

items.name: Feature attribution drift
items.summary: Which features drive predictions changes.
items.details: Compare SHAP-based importance with the baseline.
items.example: Postcode suddenly dominates a credit model.

sections.title: Evaluation metrics
sections.summary: Precision vs recall, ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC, MAE vs RMSE, BLEU vs ROUGE vs BERTScore.

items.name: Precision vs recall
items.summary: Precision: few false alarms. Recall: few misses.
items.details: Choose by the cost of each error type.
items.example: Spam quarantine → precision; cancer screening → recall.

items.name: ROC-AUC vs PR-AUC
items.summary: Both are threshold-independent; PR-AUC is more informative when positives are rare.
items.details: Pick the operating threshold separately.
items.example: Fraud models compared by PR-AUC.

items.name: MAE vs RMSE
items.summary: RMSE punishes large errors more; MAE is robust to outliers.
items.details: Choose by whether big misses are especially costly.
items.example: Storm delays inflate RMSE but not MAE.

items.name: BLEU vs ROUGE vs BERTScore vs perplexity
items.summary: Translation precision; summary recall; meaning similarity; how well a model predicts text.
items.details: Use reference-based metrics with references, and LLM-as-a-judge when references don’t exist.
items.example: BLEU for translations, ROUGE for summaries.

sections.title: Release strategies
sections.summary: Blue/green (all at once, canary, linear) vs rolling vs shadow vs A/B.

items.name: Canary
items.summary: A small share first, then the rest after a baking period.
items.details: Two steps with alarm-based rollback.
items.example: 10% for 15 minutes, then 100%.

items.name: Linear
items.summary: Equal traffic steps with baking periods.
items.details: More steps, more control.
items.example: Five steps of 20%.

items.name: Rolling
items.summary: Replace capacity in batches without a full second fleet.
items.details: Saves capacity during updates.
items.example: A 20-GPU fleet in 25% batches.

items.name: Shadow
items.summary: A copy of traffic; responses aren’t returned to users.
items.details: Validates safely before any user sees the new model.
items.example: A week of shadow traffic for a fraud model.

items.name: A/B variants
items.summary: Real users split by weight to compare outcomes.
items.details: Measures business impact.
items.example: A 90/10 split for two weeks.

sections.title: Feature engineering choices
sections.summary: Normalization vs standardization; one-hot vs label vs target encoding; log vs binning.

items.name: Normalization vs standardization
items.summary: Min-max to 0–1 vs mean 0 and standard deviation 1.
items.details: Standardization is less distorted by outliers than min-max.
items.example: Income and age standardized for KNN.

items.name: One-hot vs label vs target encoding
items.summary: Few nominal values vs ordered values vs high cardinality.
items.details: Label codes imply order; one-hot explodes with many values.
items.example: Five payment methods → one-hot.

items.name: Log transform vs binning
items.summary: Fix skew vs create ordered groups.
items.details: Log keeps values continuous; binning discretizes them.
items.example: Spend → log; age → bins by life stage.

sections.title: Chunking strategies
sections.summary: Fixed-size vs hierarchical vs semantic vs no chunking.

items.name: Fixed-size
items.summary: Token windows with overlap.
items.details: Simple and predictable; can cut ideas in half.
items.example: FAQ pages split into 300-token chunks.

items.name: Hierarchical
items.summary: Child chunks for matching, parent chunks for context.
items.details: Good for long, structured documents.
items.example: Technical manuals with sections.

items.name: Semantic
items.summary: Split where meaning changes.
items.details: Keeps related sentences together; costs more to process.
items.example: Support articles that switch topics.

items.name: No chunking
items.summary: Each file is one chunk.
items.details: For short, self-contained documents that you pre-split yourself.
items.example: One product spec per file.

sections.title: Inference parameters
sections.summary: Temperature vs top_p vs maxTokens vs stop sequences.

items.name: Temperature
items.summary: Higher means more random; lower means more deterministic.
items.details: Use low values for extraction and classification.
items.example: Temperature 0 for JSON extraction.

items.name: Top P
items.summary: Sample only from the most probable tokens up to a cumulative probability.
items.details: Another way to limit randomness; usually tune one of temperature or top P.
items.example: Top P 0.9 for varied but sensible text.

items.name: maxTokens
items.summary: Caps output length; too low truncates answers (stopReason max_tokens).
items.details: Set it to fit the expected answer length.
items.example: Short answers capped at 300 tokens.

items.name: Stop sequences
items.summary: End generation when a given string appears.
items.details: Useful for structured outputs.
items.example: Stop at “</answer>”.

sections.title: Credentials and memory pairs
sections.summary: Short-term vs long-term API keys; short-term vs long-term agent memory.

items.name: Short-term vs long-term Bedrock API keys
items.summary: Short-term: up to 12 hours, inherits the caller’s permissions. Long-term: tied to an IAM user.
items.details: Prefer IAM roles for production; set expirations on long-term keys.
items.example: A hackathon uses short-term keys.

items.name: Short-term vs long-term memory
items.summary: Within a session vs extracted across sessions.
items.details: AgentCore Memory provides both.
items.example: Remembering “tomorrow” refers to Seattle vs remembering seat preferences.
